title: Endemic species and extinction: why rare living beings need protected places

summary.text: All the wild lions of Asia live in and around one forest in Gujarat. What if that place is harmed? In this lesson you will cut a paper forest in half, flip coins to see how a small group can die out, and choose places to protect.
summary.art: A small green island alone in a blue sea with one hornbill flying above the trees, and a map of India in the corner with a dot marking the island.

intro.hook: All the wild lions of Asia live in and around one forest, the Gir forest in Gujarat. In 2020 there were 674 of them. Is 674 lions in one forest a safe number? What could go wrong?
intro.text: A crow lives in almost every town in India. If the crows of one town died, there would still be crows everywhere else. A lion-tailed macaque lives only in the rainforests of the Western Ghats. If those forests go, there is no other place with lion-tailed macaques. In this lesson you test what happens to rare species when a forest shrinks. You test whether a small group can die out by bad luck alone. Then you meet the people who have protected forests, from a village in Rajasthan in 1730 to women in Assam today.
intro.art: A lion-tailed macaque with a silver mane sitting high in a rainforest tree, looking out over misty hills.

outcomes: By the end I can say what an endemic species is, and name endemic species of India and where they live.
By the end I can explain, with my Shrinking Forest Test results, why a smaller forest holds fewer species and loses the rare ones first.
By the end I can explain why a small group in one place can die out by chance, using the Coin Years Test.
By the end I can say what extinction is, give the five main causes today, and use the steps of the Red List.
By the end I can say what national parks, sanctuaries, corridors and hotspots are, and why the size and shape of a protected area matter.
By the end I can tell how people protected forests and animals at Khejarli, Reni, Silent Valley and in Assam.
By the end I can argue both sides of a real conservation question and say what nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: One kind of living being. Members of a species can have young together, and those young can have young too.
terms.example: The house crow is one species. The jungle crow is another species. Scientists have named about 2 million species so far.
terms.art: A house crow with a grey neck and a jungle crow who is black all over, side by side on a wall, each with a name label.

terms.meaning: The variety of life in a place. It is usually measured by counting how many species live there.
terms.example: A rainforest in the Western Ghats holds thousands of species. A paddy field holds far fewer.
terms.art: A rainforest scene crowded with many different plants, birds, frogs and insects, each one a different species.

terms.meaning: Found naturally in only one place in the world, and nowhere else.
terms.example: The Nilgiri tahr is endemic to the Western Ghats. The Narcondam hornbill is endemic to one island.
terms.art: A Nilgiri tahr, a stocky wild goat, standing on a grassy cliff with a small map showing only the southern Western Ghats shaded.

terms.meaning: All the places where a species lives. A range can be as big as a continent or as small as one hill.
terms.example: The house crow's range covers most of India. The purple frog's range is a part of the Western Ghats.
terms.art: Two maps of India: one almost fully shaded for the house crow, one with a thin strip shaded for the purple frog.

terms.meaning: All the members of one species who live in one place. Scientists can count them, and the count tells us how many there are.
terms.example: The population of Asiatic lions in and around Gir was 674 in 2020.
terms.art: A group of lions resting under a tree with a forest guard counting them on a notepad from a distance.

terms.meaning: The kind of place where a species finds food, water, shelter and a place to raise young.
terms.example: The habitat of the sangai deer is the floating grass mats of Loktak lake in Manipur.
terms.art: A deer with curved antlers standing on a floating mat of grass in a wide lake.

terms.meaning: The shrinking or breaking up of a habitat, usually when people clear land for farms, roads, dams, mines or towns.
terms.example: When a grassland becomes farmland, the great Indian bustard loses the place where she nests.
terms.art: A grassland cut in half by a new road and fields, with a large long-legged bird standing in the small patch left.

terms.meaning: A species is extinct when their last member has died. An extinct species never comes back.
terms.example: The dodo of Mauritius has been extinct for more than 300 years.
terms.art: A grey outline of a dodo, drawn with dotted lines to show that nobody can see a living one.

terms.meaning: Gone from one country or region, while still alive somewhere else.
terms.example: The cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952. Cheetahs still live in Africa and a few live in Iran.
terms.art: A map of India with a faded cheetah shape on it and a map of Africa with a bright cheetah shape.

terms.meaning: At high risk of becoming extinct. The species has few members left, or the number is falling fast.
terms.example: The tiger, the Asian elephant and the lion-tailed macaque are all endangered.
terms.art: A tiger, an elephant and a lion-tailed macaque on a card with an orange 'Endangered' label.

terms.meaning: The world's list of how close each species is to extinction. It is kept by a group of scientists called the IUCN.
terms.example: On the Red List, the house crow is 'Least Concern' and the great Indian bustard is 'Critically Endangered'.
terms.art: A ladder with five steps labelled Least Concern, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered and Extinct, with a crow on the bottom step.

terms.meaning: A region with at least 1,500 plant species found nowhere else, which has already lost at least 70 out of every 100 parts of the natural plant cover that the region once had.
terms.example: The Western Ghats and Sri Lanka together are one hotspot. The world has 36 hotspots.
terms.art: A world map with 36 red patches, and the Western Ghats patch drawn larger in a circle.

terms.meaning: Land or water that the law keeps safe for wild plants and animals. Cutting trees and hunting are not allowed there.
terms.example: Silent Valley in Kerala and Kaziranga in Assam are protected areas.
terms.art: A forest with a signboard at the gate that reads 'National Park' and a guard's hut beside it.

terms.meaning: The most strictly protected kind of area in India. Nobody may live, farm or graze cattle inside.
terms.example: India's first national park was made in 1936. It is now called Jim Corbett National Park.
terms.art: A thick forest with a river and a herd of elephants, and no houses or fields anywhere.

terms.meaning: A protected area where wild animals may not be hunted. Some uses by local people, such as grazing, may be allowed.
terms.example: The Mudumalai sanctuary in Tamil Nadu became part of a tiger reserve.
terms.art: A forest edge where a few cattle graze near a signboard reading 'Wildlife Sanctuary', with deer in the trees behind.

terms.meaning: A strip of habitat that joins two protected areas, so that animals can walk from one to the other.
terms.example: Elephants in the Nilgiris use forest corridors between hills to reach food and water.
terms.art: Two forest patches joined by a narrow strip of trees, with a line of elephants walking along the strip between fields.

terms.meaning: The change in a forest near its edge. The edge is hotter, drier and windier than the middle.
terms.example: In the Bread Forest test, the rim of the bread dried first. The edge of a forest dries first too.
terms.art: A cut-away view of a forest patch with a dry, sunny outer band and a dark, damp middle.

terms.meaning: The work of keeping species and their habitats alive. It includes laws, protected areas, counting and the care of local people.
terms.example: Counting tigers, guarding nests and planting a corridor are all conservation.
terms.art: A woman fixing a camera to a tree trunk on a forest path, to photograph the animals who pass at night.

terms.meaning: A patch of forest that a village protects because of their faith. Nobody cuts trees there.
terms.example: Kerala has sacred groves called kavu. The Khasi people of Meghalaya protect the Mawphlang grove.
terms.art: A small, dense, dark patch of old trees with a stone shrine at its edge, surrounded by open fields.

explanations.concept: Biodiversity: counting the kinds of life
explanations.definition: Biodiversity is the variety of life in a place. A species is one kind of living being. The simplest way to measure biodiversity is to count the species.
explanations.description: Scientists have named about 2 million species. Many more have no name yet, because nobody has studied them. India covers about 2 in every 100 parts of the world's land. Yet India has about 7 or 8 in every 100 of the world's known species. This is because India has many kinds of habitat: snow mountains, deserts, rainforests, mangroves, grasslands and coral reefs. A count of species is only a start. Two forests can each have 10 species, but in one forest 9 of the 10 may be very rare. So scientists also ask how many members each species has.
examples: In the Shrinking Forest Test, the sheet had 10 kinds but 89 pieces. One kind had 40 pieces and two kinds had only 1.
A coral reef in the Andaman Sea can hold hundreds of species of fish in an area the size of a cricket field.
Biodiversity also means variety inside one species. India once grew many thousands of varieties of rice.
explanations.art: A page from a naturalist's notebook with small drawings of twenty different living beings, each with a tally mark count beside them.

explanations.concept: Endemic species: living in only one place
explanations.definition: An endemic species lives naturally in only one place in the world. That place can be a country, a range of hills, one lake or one island.
explanations.description: Some species have a wide range. The house crow lives across South Asia. Other species have a very small range. The Narcondam hornbill lives only on Narcondam, an island of about 7 square kilometres. About a thousand of these birds are alive. The sangai deer lives only on the floating grass of Loktak lake in Manipur. A species with a small range is not weak. They can be well fitted to their place and can live there for a very long time. But all of them share one place, so one fire, one disease or one dam can reach all of them at once.
examples: Western Ghats: lion-tailed macaque, Nilgiri tahr, Malabar grey hornbill, purple frog and the neelakurinji plant.
Islands: Narcondam hornbill on one Andaman island, and the Nicobar megapode on the Nicobar Islands.
One lake: the sangai deer of Loktak lake in Manipur.
One forest: wild Asiatic lions live only in and around Gir in Gujarat.
explanations.art: A map of India with six small pictures joined by lines to the only place where each one lives.

explanations.concept: Why islands and hilltops have species of their own
explanations.definition: A new species can form when a group is cut off from the rest of their kind for a very long time. Islands, mountain tops and old lakes cut groups off, so they hold many endemic species.
explanations.description: Birds who reach a far island cannot easily fly back and mix with the others. Over thousands of generations, the island group changes in their own way. In the end they are a new species. A cold, wet hilltop works like an island. The beings who need the cold cannot cross the hot valleys in between. The high grasslands and shola forests of the Nilgiris and the Anamalais are such 'sky islands'. The Cold Hilltop test shows what happens to such a hill when the air warms. Species can also stay on an island or a hilltop for a very long time. The purple frog is an example. Their nearest relatives live on the Seychelles islands, far across the sea. India and the Seychelles were joined about 65 million years ago, so the frogs have been separated from their relatives for a very long time.
examples: Madagascar has been an island for about 88 million years. Lemurs live there and nowhere else.
In the Western Ghats, most species of frog are endemic.
The Nilgiri tahr lives on high grassy cliffs. Hot lowland forest separates one herd's hills from the next.
explanations.art: A side view of three hills rising out of a layer of cloud, each top with a different small animal on the summit, like islands in a white sea.

explanations.definition: Some parts of India hold far more endemic species than others. Four of them are the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the Sundarbans, the hills of Northeast India and the Western Ghats.
explanations.description: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie far out in the sea, so many of their birds and reptiles are endemic. Coral reefs grow around them. A reef is built by corals, who are tiny animals with stony homes. The Sundarbans, shared by West Bengal and Bangladesh, is the largest mangrove forest in the world. Mangroves are trees who can grow in salty mud, and tigers there swim between islands. The hills of Northeast India hold the hoolock gibbon, who is India's only ape, and the sangai deer. The Western Ghats run for about 1,600 kilometres through six states, from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu. They are older than the Himalaya.
examples: Andaman and Nicobar Islands: the Narcondam hornbill, the Nicobar megapode and coral reefs.
Sundarbans: mangrove trees with roots that stick up out of the mud to take in air.
Northeast India: the hoolock gibbon, who is India's only ape, and the sangai deer, who is found only in Manipur.
Western Ghats: the lion-tailed macaque, the Nilgiri tahr and the purple frog.
explanations.art: A map of India with four regions coloured: the island chain in the east, the delta in Bengal, the north-eastern hills and the long strip down the west coast.

explanations.definition: A biodiversity hotspot is a region with at least 1,500 plant species found nowhere else. The region must also have lost at least 70 out of every 100 parts of the natural plant cover that the region once had.
explanations.description: The British scientist Norman Myers gave this idea its name in 1988. He asked where money for conservation would save the most species. Endemic species are not spread evenly over the Earth. They are crowded into a few regions. Today 36 regions count as hotspots. Their remaining natural habitat covers only about 2 and a half parts in 100 of the Earth's land. Yet more than half of the world's plant species are endemic to these regions. Four hotspots include parts of India: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland, which includes the Nicobar Islands. In the game Two Safe Squares, one square holds three rare species. Protecting that one square saves all three.
examples: The Western Ghats and Sri Lanka form one hotspot.
The Indo-Burma hotspot includes most of Northeast India.
A hotspot has two parts to its meaning: many endemic species, and great loss already.
explanations.art: A world map where 36 small regions glow red, with a magnifying glass over the west coast of India.

explanations.concept: Extinction: when the last one dies
explanations.definition: A species is extinct when their last member has died. Extinction cannot be undone. A species can also be locally extinct, which means gone from one region but alive elsewhere.
explanations.description: Extinction has always happened. More than 99 in every 100 species who ever lived are extinct. Five times in the Earth's past, most species died out within a short time. The last time was 66 million years ago, when the large dinosaurs died. What is new today is the speed and the cause. Scientists estimate that species are now dying out tens to hundreds of times faster than before people spread across the Earth. The dodo was a large flightless bird of Mauritius. Sailors first landed there in 1598, and the last sure sighting of a dodo was in 1662. In India, the cheetah was declared extinct in 1952. It is hard to be sure a species is gone. The forest owlet of central India was not seen after 1884. In 1997 the scientists Pamela Rasmussen and Ben King found forest owlets alive in Maharashtra.
examples: Extinct: the dodo of Mauritius, and the passenger pigeon of North America, whose last bird died in a zoo in 1914.
Locally extinct: the cheetah in India since 1952.
Found again: the forest owlet in 1997, after 113 years.
explanations.art: A museum shelf with a dodo skeleton, and beside it a photograph of a small living owl pinned up with the date 1997.

explanations.definition: Most species in danger today are in danger for one or more of five reasons: habitat loss, taking too many, species brought in from elsewhere, pollution and a changing climate.
explanations.description: Habitat loss is the biggest cause. A forest is cleared for a farm, or cut into pieces by roads. The second cause is taking too many, by hunting, fishing or collecting. The third is species that people carry to new places. Rats, pigs and monkeys brought by ships ate the eggs of the dodo. The fourth is pollution. In the 1990s, a medicine given to cattle poisoned most of India's vultures who fed on the dead cattle. The fifth is the warming climate. Warm sea water makes corals turn white and die. On a mountain, cold-loving species move higher as the air warms, until no higher ground is left. Often two or three causes work together.
examples: Great Indian bustard: grassland lost to farms, and birds killed by flying into power lines. About 130 are left.
Dodo: hunted by sailors, and their eggs eaten by animals from the ships.
Corals around Lakshadweep and the Andamans: bleached by warm water in very hot years.
explanations.art: Five small panels: a bulldozer at a forest edge, a net full of fish, a rat beside a nest of eggs, a pipe pouring dirty water into a river, and a thermometer in the sea beside white coral.

explanations.concept: A smaller forest holds fewer species
explanations.definition: The smaller an area of habitat is, the fewer species it holds. The rare species and the species with a small range are lost first.
explanations.description: In the Shrinking Forest Test, the half sheet still held about 8 of the 10 kinds. The quarter held about 6. The kinds that went missing first were the ones with only 1 or 2 pieces. A common species is found in every part of a forest, so any part that is left still has some. A rare species lives in only a few spots, and the part that is left may hold none of them. Scientists have counted species on islands and in forests of many sizes, and they find the same pattern. A rough rule is that when 90 in every 100 parts of a habitat are lost, about half the species are lost. This also means that the first cut can look harmless. Most species are still there. The ones that went missing were rare, so hardly anyone would have noticed them even before the cut.
examples: In the Shrinking Forest Test: the whole sheet had 10 kinds, the half about 8, the quarter about 6 and the sixteenth about 3.
Large islands hold more species of birds than small islands of the same kind.
A city park holds fewer species than a large forest, even when every tree in the park is protected.
explanations.art: A square forest drawn four times, each time half the size, with a row of animal pictures under each that gets shorter as the forest shrinks.

explanations.concept: Small numbers are risky by themselves
explanations.definition: A small population can die out by chance alone, even when nobody hunts them and their habitat is safe. One bad year, one disease or a few years with few young can end a small group.
explanations.description: In the Coin Years Test, both groups followed the same rule, and on average each adult left one young. The group with room for 4 died out in most runs. The group with room for 16 rarely did. With 4 coins, all 4 land tails about 1 time in 16. With 16 coins, all tails happens about 1 time in 65,000. Real animals face the same risk. In a small group, a few bad seasons can leave too few young. One disease can reach every member, because they all live together. In 2018, more than 20 lions in one part of Gir died within weeks from a disease carried by dogs and ticks. Close relatives also have to mate with each other in a small group, and their young can be less healthy. So scientists want every rare species to have a large number, and to live in more than one place.
examples: Asiatic lions: 674 in 2020, all in and around one forest.
Great Indian bustard: about 130, most of them in Rajasthan.
Narcondam hornbill: about a thousand birds on one island.
explanations.art: Two groups of coins on a table: four coins all showing tails on the left, and sixteen coins with a mix of heads and tails on the right.

explanations.concept: Measuring the risk: the Red List
explanations.definition: The Red List places each species on a step, from Least Concern to Extinct. The steps in between are Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered.
explanations.description: A step is picked from measurements. It does not depend on how much people like an animal. Scientists use three measures. How many adults are left? How fast is the number falling? How small is the range? A species with fewer than 250 adults who are still falling in number can be Critically Endangered. So can a species who has lost 80 in every 100 members in ten years. The list is checked again and again, and a species can move up or down. A species can move to a safer step when things get better. In 2008 the Indian rhinoceros moved from Endangered to Vulnerable, because their numbers had grown. More than 40,000 species are now listed as threatened with extinction. Most species have never been checked at all.
examples: Least Concern: house crow, peafowl.
Vulnerable: Indian rhinoceros, snow leopard.
Endangered: tiger, Asian elephant, lion-tailed macaque, Nilgiri tahr.
Critically Endangered: great Indian bustard, gharial.
explanations.art: A ladder leaning on a wall with a different Indian animal on each step and the word Extinct on the ground below the ladder.

explanations.concept: Protected areas: size, shape and joins
explanations.definition: A protected area is land or water where the law protects wild plants and animals. India has national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, tiger reserves and biosphere reserves.
explanations.description: India's main wildlife law is the Wild Life (Protection) Act of 1972. India now has more than 100 national parks and more than 550 wildlife sanctuaries. Together, protected areas cover about 5 in every 100 parts of India's land. Their size and shape matter. A small patch loses rare species, as the Shrinking Forest Test shows. A small patch is also mostly edge. In the Bread Forest test, the 16 small squares dried right through while the whole slice stayed soft in the middle. A forest edge is hotter, drier and windier than the middle, and some species cannot live there. So one large area usually keeps more forest species than many small ones. Where a large area is not possible, a corridor of trees can join two smaller ones. Then animals can move between them, and a group that dies out in one can be replaced from the other.
examples: A tiger reserve has a core, where nobody lives, and a buffer around the core, where people and wildlife share the land.
On the highway through the Pench forest in central India, long bridges let tigers and deer walk underneath the traffic.
A sacred grove is a small protected area kept by a village, sometimes for hundreds of years.
explanations.art: A map of a tiger reserve with a dark green core, a light green buffer around the core, and a thin green corridor leading to a second forest.

explanations.concept: People who protect forests and animals
explanations.definition: Many forests and species in India are alive today because ordinary people protected them, often before any law did.
explanations.description: In 1730, at Khejarli in Rajasthan, the king's men came to cut khejri trees. A Bishnoi woman, Amrita Devi, held on to a tree and was killed. In all, about 363 Bishnoi people are said to have died protecting the trees, and the king then stopped the cutting. In 1974, at Reni in the Himalaya, Gaura Devi and the women of her village stood between the loggers and the trees. This was part of the Chipko movement. 'Chipko' means 'hug'. In Kerala in the 1970s, a dam was planned that would have drowned the rainforest of Silent Valley. Teachers, scientists and writers spoke against the dam for years. Among them were the poet Sugathakumari and the botanist Janaki Ammal. The dam was dropped in 1983, and Silent Valley became a national park in 1984. In Assam, the biologist Purnima Devi Barman found that villagers were cutting the trees where hargila storks nested. From 2007 she worked with the women of those villages. They became the Hargila Army, which news reports say now has thousands of women. News reports say the nests in their villages rose from about 28 in 2007 to about 200 by 2019.
examples: Khejarli, Rajasthan, 1730: Amrita Devi and the Bishnoi.
Reni, Uttarakhand, 1974: Gaura Devi and the Chipko movement.
Silent Valley, Kerala, 1973 to 1984: a dam stopped by a public campaign.
Kamrup, Assam, from 2007: Purnima Devi Barman and the Hargila Army.
Pangti, Nagaland, 2013: a village that had hunted Amur falcons began to protect them.
explanations.art: Four small scenes in a row: women holding tree trunks in a desert village, women standing before trees in the mountains, a crowd with banners beside a rainforest river, and women in woven shawls under a tree full of large storks.

explanations.concept: Should people live inside protected areas?
explanations.description: Many protected areas were made by moving villages out. Many other forests have been protected by the people who live in them. Which works better is still argued about. India's Forest Rights Act of 2006 gives forest peoples the right to stay on and care for their forest land.
examples: The Bishnoi protect wild blackbuck and chinkara in their own villages and fields.
The Maldhari herders have lived among the lions of Gir for generations.
Some tiger reserves have paid villages to move out of the core, so that tigers and deer have land with no cattle.

perspectives.explanation: Tigers and other large animals need areas with no people, no cattle and no roads. Where villages moved out of a core, deer and tigers increased.

perspectives.who: Many forest peoples and social scientists
perspectives.explanation: People who depend on a forest guard that forest best. Moving them out is unjust, and it can leave the forest with no defenders against mines and dams.
It depends on the place and the species. A strict core for the animals who need it, and shared forest around the core, can serve both.

explanations.art: A forest village of a few thatched houses with cattle, and a tiger's pugmarks on the path beside the houses.

explanations.concept: How many species are there, and how fast are they going?
explanations.description: Nobody knows how many species live on Earth. About 2 million have names. One well-known estimate is about 9 million, not counting bacteria. Other estimates are much higher. Because most species are unknown, nobody can count extinctions exactly. A group of scientists working for the United Nations estimated in 2019 that about 1 million species are at risk. That number is an estimate built from the groups that have been studied. The purple frog was named by scientists only in 2003, though people living in those hills already knew the frog.
examples: New species are named every year in India, mostly frogs, insects and plants.
Birds and mammals are almost all known. Insects, fungi and deep-sea animals are mostly unknown.
Some species probably die out before anybody has named them.
explanations.art: A large shelf of labelled jars where only the first few have labels and the rest, stretching into the distance, are blank.

agreed.text: Extinction is real and cannot be undone.
agreed.evidence: Fossils show many species who no longer live anywhere. In our own time, the last passenger pigeon died in a zoo in 1914, and no dodo has been seen since 1662.

agreed.text: Species are dying out much faster now than before people spread across the Earth.
agreed.evidence: Scientists compare the extinctions recorded in the last 500 years with the rate seen in fossils. The exact size of the difference is argued about, but all careful estimates find a large one.

agreed.text: Habitat loss is the biggest cause of extinction today.
agreed.evidence: The Red List records the threats to each species checked. Loss of habitat to farming, logging and building is listed for more species than any other threat.

agreed.text: A smaller area of habitat holds fewer species, and species with small ranges are at the greatest risk.
agreed.evidence: Counts on islands and in forest patches of many sizes show the same pattern. In Brazil, patches of forest left among cattle farms lost many species of forest birds within 15 years.

agreed.text: Protection can work. Species have come back from very small numbers.
agreed.evidence: India counted 1,411 tigers in 2006 and 3,682 in 2022. The Indian rhinoceros rose from fewer than 200 in the early 1900s to more than 4,000.

challenging.claim: Extinction is natural, so people need not try to stop it.
challenging.who: R. Alexander Pyron, an American biologist, in a newspaper essay in 2017, and others before him
challenging.for: More than 99 in every 100 species who ever lived are extinct. New species formed after every great extinction in the past.
challenging.against: Species are now dying out far faster than new ones can form. Recovery after past extinctions took millions of years. Most biologists also say that each species matters for their own sake.
challenging.context: This card is about the view that extinction is a normal part of life on Earth and needs no action.

challenging.claim: One large protected area is always better than several small ones.
challenging.who: Jared Diamond, an American scientist, in 1975
challenging.for: A large area keeps large animals, has less edge, and holds bigger populations that are safer from chance. The Bread Forest test shows the edge problem.
challenging.against: Daniel Simberloff and Lawrence Abele showed in 1976 that several small areas in different places can together hold more species. One fire or disease also cannot reach them all.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a country should make one big protected area or several small ones.

challenging.claim: A lost species should be brought back from another country.
challenging.who: The planners of India's cheetah project, which brought African cheetahs to Kuno National Park from 2022
challenging.for: Cheetahs once lived in India's grasslands, and people caused their extinction here. Bringing them back may also win protection for grasslands.
challenging.against: The cheetahs brought are from Africa, and India's own cheetahs are gone. Some scientists say the space is too small. Several cheetahs died in the first years.
challenging.context: This card is about bringing cheetahs from Africa to India, 70 years after cheetahs became extinct in India.

challenging.claim: Money should go to hotspots first, not to every forest equally.
challenging.who: Norman Myers, a British scientist, in 1988
challenging.for: Hotspots hold more than half the world's endemic plants on a tiny share of the land. Each rupee spent there protects more species.
challenging.against: Deserts, grasslands and cold seas have fewer species but unique ones. Places outside hotspots also clean water and store carbon. People live in all of them.
challenging.context: This card is about how to choose which places to protect when there is not enough money for all.

challenging.claim: An animal is protected only by keeping people far away.
challenging.who: A common belief, and the plan behind many early national parks
challenging.for: Hunting and cattle grazing do reduce wild animals. Some shy species leave when people come near.
challenging.against: The Bishnoi, the Hargila Army and the village of Pangti protect animals beside their own homes. Many sacred groves are older than any national park.
challenging.context: This card is about whether people can share their land with the other wild animals.

big_questions.q: The dodo died out before anyone drew a careful picture of a living one. What exactly was lost when the last dodo died?
big_questions.hint: Think of what a species is: a body, a way of living, and millions of years of history. Could any of these be made again?

big_questions.q: In the Shrinking Forest Test, the half sheet looked almost as full as the whole. How would you know if a real forest had lost species?
big_questions.hint: Think of who went missing first in your test. Would a visitor ever have seen them?

big_questions.q: A lioness kills a herder's buffalo. Who should pay for the lions of Gir: the herder, the state or the whole world?
big_questions.hint: The lions belong to no single person, and people everywhere gain from knowing they are alive. But when a lioness kills a buffalo, only one family loses the animal and the money. Think about whether it is fair that one family carries that cost.

big_questions.q: There is not enough money to save every species. How should people choose? Should people choose at all?
big_questions.hint: Some say save the most species for each rupee. Some say save the ones nobody else will. Some say no species should be given up.

big_questions.q: Humans are one species among about 2 million named ones. Does one species have the right to decide which others live?
big_questions.hint: People already decide, every time land is cleared or protected. The question is how to decide well.

big_questions.q: Is a species still alive if the last members live only in a zoo?
big_questions.hint: Think of what an animal does in the wild that she cannot do in a zoo: hunt, migrate, choose a mate, teach her young.

story.title: The Only Lions
story.note: The lions and the sickness are real. In September and October 2018, 23 lions died in the Dalkhania range of the Gir forest in Gujarat, from a virus that dogs carry and from a disease spread by ticks. Forest staff caught other lions and vaccinated them, and news reports say dogs and cattle in nearby villages were vaccinated too. The count of 523 lions is from 2015. The Maldharis are real herding people who live in hamlets called nesses inside Gir, and the forest department does pay for cattle killed by lions. Gir has had women forest guards since 2007. Rudi, Ba, Hansaben, Dholi and Kalu are imagined, and so is everything they say and do.
text: Rudi's family lived in a ness, a hamlet of six mud houses inside the Gir forest in Gujarat. They were Maldharis, people who keep buffaloes. Every morning Rudi's grandmother, whom everyone called Ba, milked eleven buffaloes. Every morning Rudi fed the calves. Her favourite was a pale calf called Dholi, who liked to chew the end of Rudi's plait.

One night in August 2018, at the end of the rains, the dog Kalu barked and would not stop. There was a crash at the thorn fence, and a sound Rudi had never heard a buffalo make. Ba came out with a lantern and a stick, shouting. By the time the lantern reached the fence, there was a gap in the thorns and a wide trail through the wet grass.
"Dholi," said Rudi.
"A lioness," said Ba. She looked at the paw marks for a while. "She has cubs. See how deep she pressed. She was hunting alone, for more than herself."
"I don't care if she has cubs!"
Ba mended the fence and did not answer.

In the morning a forest guard came on a motorcycle to write the report, so that the family would be paid for the calf. Her name was Hansaben. She had grown up in a ness herself. She measured the paw marks and filled in a form.
"How much will they pay?" asked Rudi.
"Enough for another calf."

"It won't be Dholi." Rudi kicked the dust. "Why do we have to keep lions here at all? On television there are lions in Africa. Hundreds of them, lying about in the grass. People can go and look at those."
Hansaben signed the form. "Those are Africa's lions," she said. "I have work in Dalkhania. Ask me another day."

For three weeks Rudi did not ask. She fed the calves and did not give any of them a name. At night, when the lions roared from the riverbed, Ba would say, "There she is," as if the lioness were a neighbour. Rudi pulled the quilt over her ears.

Then, in late September, the jeeps began. They went past the ness towards Dalkhania, in the east of the forest, and they came back carrying cages covered in green cloth. Men in masks rode in the back. Hansaben's motorcycle went by twice a day and did not stop.
When she did stop, it was for water. Her eyes were red. Ba gave her buttermilk and made her sit down.

"Lions are dying in Dalkhania," Hansaben said. "It is a sickness. The doctors say it came from dogs, and ticks carry a second one. Twenty-three lions so far. We are catching the others, to give them an injection before the sickness reaches them."
Rudi had wished the lions gone every night for three weeks. Now she found that she wanted a number.
"Twenty-three out of how many?"
"The last count was five hundred and twenty-three."
"That still leaves five hundred."
"Yes."
"And in the other forests?"
Hansaben looked at her. Then she picked up a twig and drew a circle in the dust, about as wide as a thali.

"This is Gir, and the land around it," she said. "Long ago there were lions like ours from Greece all the way to Bihar. People hunted them and ploughed the land. By my great-grandmother's time, the only ones left were inside this circle. People say there were fewer than fifty."
She tapped the dust outside the circle, on one side and then on the other.
"Here, none. Here, none. No other forest in India. No other country in Asia. Not one."
Rudi looked at the circle. A circle that size could be rubbed out with one foot.
"So if the sickness goes all the way across..."
"Then there are no lions of Asia. Not here and not anywhere, because for them anywhere is here."
Rudi thought about the lioness. She did not want to, but she did. She thought of the deep paw marks, and of cubs waiting under a bush somewhere near Dalkhania.
"Kalu barks at the lions every night," she said slowly. "He goes right up to the fence. The dogs of every ness do."
"I know," said Hansaben. "Next week the doctors are coming to the nesses to inject the dogs and the cattle. Half the dogs will run off and hide. Nobody can catch a ness dog."
"I can catch Kalu," said Rudi. "I can catch all of them. They know me."

The next week she did. She caught Kalu first and held his head while the needle went in, so that the other dogs could see he lived through it. Then she rode from ness to ness in the doctors' jeep, calling each dog by name. It took four days. She was bitten once, not badly.
On the last evening she came home after dark. Ba was milking. From the riverbed came a roar. It began low, rose, and ended in a row of short grunts.
"There she is," said Ba.
Rudi listened until it stopped.
"Are you still angry with her?" Ba asked.
"Yes," said Rudi. She picked up the calves' bucket. "I just want her to be there."
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn comes when Hansaben draws the circle in the dust. Rudi had thought of lions as something the world has plenty of. The circle shows her that these lions are endemic to one place. A sickness that crosses one forest would cross the whole range of the species. So a danger to the place is a danger to every lion there is. Rudi does not stop being angry about her calf. She acts because she now knows what 'only here' means.
ask: Rudi said that people could go and look at the lions in Africa. What did she not know yet?
Why is one sickness more dangerous to the lions of Gir than to the crows of India?
Hansaben said, 'For them anywhere is here.' Say that in your own words.
Rudi was still angry at the end. Can you want an animal to live and still be angry with her?
Some people want to move a few lions to a second forest far away. How would that help? Who might not like it?

games.title: Two Safe Squares: which two squares should be protected?
games.context: This is a paper game about choosing places to protect. You will find out which two squares save the most species. A forest map has 9 squares and 12 made-up species. You can keep only 2 squares safe, and the other 7 will be cleared.

printables.title: The forest map: draw a square and split it into 9 squares
12 two-sided species cards to cut out (the back says how safe she is)

items.f: A common babbler, a small bird. Lives in squares B, C, D, E, G.
items.b: Lives in 5 squares. She is hard to lose, because a protected square will often hold her.

items.f: A squirrel. Lives in squares A, C, D, E, G, I.
items.b: Lives in 6 squares. She is hard to lose, because a protected square will often hold her.

items.f: A langur, a monkey with a long tail. Lives in squares B, F, G, H, I.
items.b: Lives in 5 squares. She is hard to lose, because a protected square will often hold her.

items.f: A barbet, a small green bird. Lives in squares C, D, G.
items.b: Lives in 3 squares. She is lost only if all 3 squares are cleared.

items.f: An otter. Lives in squares A, F.
items.b: Lives in 2 squares. She is lost only if both squares are cleared.

items.f: A brown frog. Lives in squares D, H.
items.b: Lives in 2 squares. She is lost only if both squares are cleared.

items.f: A rare orchid. Lives in square D.
items.b: Lives in one square only. If square D is cleared, she is gone for ever.

items.f: A tree lizard. Lives in square D.
items.b: Lives in one square only. If square D is cleared, she is gone for ever.

items.f: A tiny blue frog. Lives in square D.
items.b: Lives in one square only. If square D is cleared, she is gone for ever.

items.f: A macaque. Lives in square I.
items.b: Lives in one square only. If square I is cleared, she is gone for ever.

items.f: A hornbill. Lives in square F.
items.b: Lives in one square only. If square F is cleared, she is gone for ever.

items.f: A flying squirrel. Lives in square B.
items.b: Lives in one square only. If square B is cleared, she is gone for ever.

rules: The 12 species and the map are made up. Each card shows the squares where one species lives.
Draw the map and lay the 12 cards beside it, face up.
Each player secretly writes 2 squares to protect. Every other square will be cleared.
Reveal the squares. A species is saved if she lives in at least one protected square.
Score 1 point for each species saved. If two players tie, the player who saved more species who live in one square only wins.
Play 2 rounds. The player with the most points wins. Playing alone: try to beat your own score in round 2.

setup.art: A hand-drawn square split into nine squares labelled A to I, with twelve small cards laid in a row beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the map and lay out the 12 cards.

setup.art: The map with two squares shaded green and the other seven crossed out in red pencil.
setup.caption: 2. Protect 2 squares. Clear the other 7.

setup.art: Species cards sorted into two piles: saved and lost, with a score written on a notepad.
setup.caption: 3. Sort the cards into saved and lost, and score.

flow.do: 1. Draw a square about 15 centimetres wide. 2. Split it into 9 squares, in 3 rows of 3. 3. Write the letters A to I in the squares, row by row. 4. Cut out the 12 cards and lay them beside the map.
flow.say: This is a forest of nine squares. Twelve species live in it. Each card shows the squares where one species lives.
flow.kid: Draw a big square. Split it into 9 squares. Write A to I in the squares. Cut out the 12 cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Safe Squares. Here you draw the forest map and cut out the 12 species cards.

flow.do: 1. Explain that only 2 squares can be protected, and the other 7 will be cleared for farms. 2. Ask which 2 squares your child would protect. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Only two squares can be kept safe. The other seven will be cleared. Which two will you protect? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You can protect only 2 squares. Which 2 will you pick? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why those two squares?
good: The squares with the most species. (A fair guess. The game will test it.)
The squares where rare species live.
I do not know yet. I need to look at the cards.

flow.context: This step of Two Safe Squares is for guessing. You guess which 2 squares to protect, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Take each card in turn. 2. Make a tally mark in every square where she lives, as the card shows. 3. Count the marks in each square. 4. Circle the square with the most marks.
flow.say: Let us find out who lives where. Make a tally mark in every square where she lives. Then count the marks in each square.
flow.kid: Take each card. Make a tally mark in every square where she lives. Count the marks in each square. Circle the biggest count.
flow.parent: Square D holds 7 species, and three of them (the orchid, the tree lizard and the tiny blue frog) live nowhere else. The other squares hold 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 4, 2 and 3 species, in the order A, B, C, E, F, G, H, I.
flow.context: This step of Two Safe Squares maps who lives where. You write each species into her squares and count how many species live in each square.

flow.do: 1. Now choose your 2 squares and write them down. 2. Cross out the other 7 squares. 3. Go through the cards. A species is saved if she lives in at least one protected square. 4. Count your saved species.
flow.say: Choose your two squares. Everything outside them will be cleared. Which species are saved? Which are lost? Count the points.
flow.kid: Choose 2 squares. Cross out the other 7. Sort the cards into saved and lost. Count your points.

ask.q: Which species were lost? What do they have in common?
good: They live in only one or two squares.
They lived in squares I did not protect.

flow.context: This is round 1 of Two Safe Squares. You protect 2 squares, clear the rest, and count which species are saved.

flow.do: 1. Round 2: try to find the best pair of squares. 2. Check every pair that includes square D, because D holds 7 species. 3. For each pair, count the saved species. 4. Write the best score you find.
flow.say: Now try again. Can you find a pair of squares that saves more species? Check the pairs with D first.
flow.kid: Round 2. Look for a better pair. Try every pair that includes D. Count the saved species each time.
flow.parent: The best pair is D and F. Together they save 10 of the 12 species, and only the macaque and the flying squirrel are lost. The two richest squares, D and G, save only 8. G adds just one new species, the langur, because the babbler, the squirrel and the barbet are already safe in D.

check.q: Why did the two squares with the most species not save the most species?
options: Many of their species were the same ones
Cleared squares were chosen at random
Rich squares cannot be protected
check.why: Squares D and G share the babbler, the squirrel and the barbet, so G added only the langur. Square F added three new species: the langur, the otter and the hornbill. The first answer is right, because what matters is how many different species the two squares hold together. The third answer forgets that any square can be protected.

flow.context: This is round 2 of Two Safe Squares. You search for the pair of squares that saves the most species.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 2. Ask which species a country should worry about most, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Which species would worry you most?

ask.q: Why is a species who lives in one square more at risk than one who lives in five?
good: Clearing one square removes all of her.
A fire, a disease or a road in one place can reach all of her.
The one who lives in five squares has a second chance.

flow.parent: Real planners do the same sum. They ask which set of places holds the most different species, and they look hardest at species who live in only one place. This is the idea behind biodiversity hotspots.
flow.context: This is the last step of Two Safe Squares. You explain which pair of squares saved the most species, and why counting species in each square was not enough.

games.title: Climb the Red List: which step is she on?
games.context: This is a card game about the Red List, the world's list of how close each species is to extinction. Each card gives facts about one made-up species. You work out her step on the Red List ladder.

printables.title: 12 two-sided species cards to cut out (the back gives the step and the working)

items.f: A river fish. About 40,000 adults. Numbers are steady. Lives in many rivers.
items.b: Least Concern. 40,000 adults is 0 points. Total 0.

items.f: A forest owl. About 12,000 adults. Numbers are falling. Lives in many forests.
items.b: Near Threatened. 12,000 adults is 0 points, falling adds 1. Total 1.

items.f: A grassland lark. About 6,000 adults. Numbers are falling. Lives in many grasslands.
items.b: Vulnerable. 6,000 adults is 1 point, falling adds 1. Total 2.

items.f: A hill frog. About 5,000 adults. Numbers are steady. All live on one hill.
items.b: Vulnerable. 5,000 adults is 1 point, one place adds 1. Total 2.

items.f: A mountain goat. About 1,800 adults. Numbers are steady. Lives on several mountains.
items.b: Vulnerable. 1,800 adults is 2 points. Total 2.

items.f: A marsh deer. About 900 adults. Numbers are falling. All live in one lake.
items.b: Critically Endangered. 900 adults is 2 points, falling adds 1, one place adds 1. Total 4.

items.f: A river crocodile. About 200 adults. Numbers are falling. Lives in three rivers.
items.b: Critically Endangered. 200 adults is 3 points, falling adds 1. Total 4.

items.f: A forest macaque. About 3,500 adults. Numbers are falling. All live in one range of hills.
items.b: Endangered. 3,500 adults is 1 point, falling adds 1, one place adds 1. Total 3.

items.f: A coral fish. About 90,000 adults. Numbers are falling. Lives along a whole coast.
items.b: Near Threatened. 90,000 adults is 0 points, falling adds 1. Total 1.

items.f: An island bird. About 400 adults. Numbers are steady. All live on one island.
items.b: Endangered. 400 adults is 2 points, one place adds 1. Total 3.

items.f: A forest tortoise. About 15,000 adults. Numbers are rising. Lives in many forests.
items.b: Least Concern. 15,000 adults is 0 points. Total 0.

items.f: A mountain orchid. About 140 adults. Numbers are steady. Lives in three valleys.
items.b: Endangered. 140 adults is 3 points. Total 3.

printables.title: The ladder to copy: five steps and the point rules
items: Step 1. Count the adults. More than 10,000 is 0 points. From 2,500 to 10,000 is 1 point. From 250 to 2,500 is 2 points. Fewer than 250 is 3 points.
Step 3. All the adults live in one place adds 1 point.
Add the points. 0 is Least Concern. 1 is Near Threatened. 2 is Vulnerable. 3 is Endangered. 4 or more is Critically Endangered.

rules: All 12 species are made up. The real Red List uses more measures than these three, so this is a simple game version.
Copy the ladder and the point rules onto a sheet of paper. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, facts side up.
On your turn, read the top card. Add the points with the three rules, and say which step she is on.
Turn the card over. Score 1 point if your step is right.
If you are wrong, find the rule you missed and say it aloud. Then put the card at the bottom of the pile.
When every card has been read once, the player with the most points wins. Playing alone: play again another day and beat your score.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a ladder of five steps labelled from Least Concern at the bottom to Critically Endangered at the top.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the ladder and the point rules.

setup.art: A child reading a species card with facts about adults, trend and range, with a pencil adding points on a notepad.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card and add up the points.

setup.art: A card turned over to show the answer, with a score written on a sheet beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over and check your step.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. Shuffle them. 2. Copy the ladder and the 3 point rules onto a sheet of paper. 3. Read the rules aloud together. 4. Put the cards in a pile, facts side up.
flow.say: The Red List shows how close each species is to extinction. We will use three clues: how many adults there are, whether the number is falling, and whether all of them live in one place.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Copy the ladder and the point rules. Put the cards in a pile.
flow.context: This is the first step of Climb the Red List. Here you copy the ladder and the point rules, and set out the cards.

flow.do: 1. Read this example aloud. A species has 150 adults, all in one forest, and the number is falling. 2. Ask which step she is on, and why. 3. Write down the guess and the reason. 4. Check it with the rules: 3 points for under 250, plus 1 for falling, plus 1 for one place is 5. The top step is 4 points, so she is Critically Endangered.
flow.say: A species has 150 adults. All of them live in one forest, and the number is falling. Which step of the ladder is she on? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A species has 150 adults. All live in one forest. The number is falling. Which step is she on?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Critically Endangered, because 150 is very few and they are all in one place.
Near the top, because the number is falling.

flow.context: This step of Climb the Red List is for guessing. You guess the step of one species from three clues, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Take the top card. Read it aloud. 2. Add the points with the three rules. 3. Say her step. 4. Turn the card over. Score 1 point if you are right. 5. Go through all 12 cards.
flow.say: Read the card. How many points for the number of adults? Is the number falling? Do all of them live in one place? Add them up.
flow.kid: Read the card. Add the points. Say her step. Turn the card over. Score 1 if you are right.
flow.parent: Answers. River fish: Least Concern. Forest owl and coral fish: Near Threatened. Grassland lark, hill frog and mountain goat: Vulnerable. Forest macaque, island bird and mountain orchid: Endangered. Marsh deer and river crocodile: Critically Endangered. Forest tortoise: Least Concern.
flow.context: This step of Climb the Red List is the game itself. You work out the step of each of the 12 species.

flow.do: 1. Count your score. 2. Find the hill frog card and the mountain goat card. The frog has more adults, but both are on the same step. 3. Ask why.
flow.say: Find the hill frog card and the mountain goat card. Which has more adults? Which step is each on?
flow.kid: Find the two cards. Check the step of each.

ask.q: The hill frog has 5,000 adults and the mountain goat has 1,800. Why is the frog on the same step?
good: All the frogs live on one hill, so one event could reach all of them.
Living in one place adds a point of risk, even with more adults.

check.q: A species has 8,000 adults, and the number is steady. All of them live in one valley. Which step?
options: Least Concern
Vulnerable
Endangered
check.why: 8,000 adults is 1 point. Living in one valley adds 1 point. The total is 2, which is Vulnerable. Choosing Least Concern means counting only the adults and forgetting how small the range is.

flow.context: This step of Climb the Red List compares two species. You find out how living in one place changes a species' step.

experiments.title: The Shrinking Forest Test: how many kinds are left when a forest is cut to half?
experiments.context: In this experiment you find out whether cutting a forest in half loses half of its kinds. A sheet of newspaper is the forest. Ten kinds of small kitchen pieces are ten species, some common and some rare. You scatter them, then count how many kinds are left on half the sheet, a quarter, an eighth and a sixteenth.
experiments.question: A forest has 10 species, some common and some rare. When the forest is cut to half its size, how many of the 10 species are still there? How many are there when only a sixteenth is left?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When only half the sheet is kept, how many of the 10 kinds will be on it: about 5, more than 5, or fewer than 5? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: The parts to keep are marked before the pieces are scattered, so nobody can choose a lucky part. The same 89 pieces are used each time. Scatter and count 3 times, because one scatter can be a fluke.
results_table: Which kinds were missing from the half

materials.item: one full sheet of newspaper, opened out
a marker pen or a sketch pen

ten kinds of small dry pieces from the kitchen, in these numbers: 40 rice grains, 20 masoor dal, 10 whole moong, 6 chana, 4 rajma, 3 groundnuts, 2 peppercorns, 2 cloves, 1 cardamom and 1 dry red chilli. Any ten kinds will do, such as other dals, beads or buttons, if the numbers are the same.
a steel tumbler
a bed, a mat or a folded bedsheet to lay the newspaper on
paper and a pencil for the table

schedule.what: Fold and mark the sheet. Guess. Scatter the 89 pieces 3 times and count the kinds on each part. Find the averages and explain them. Then test one endemic kind.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for 3 scatters. Find the average number of kinds on the half, the quarter, the eighth and the sixteenth. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: average number of kinds left out of 10
example_chart.x: Part of the sheet that is kept
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: An opened newspaper sheet on a bed, with fold lines dividing the sheet into 16 parts, the left half outlined in thick pen and marked KEEP, and smaller boxes marked inside its top corner.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the sheet into 16 parts. Mark the half, the quarter, the eighth and the sixteenth.

setup.art: A child's hand tipping a steel tumbler above the newspaper, with rice, dal, chana and a red chilli falling and scattering over the sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Scatter the 89 pieces over the whole sheet.

setup.art: A child pointing at pieces on the marked half of the sheet and writing numbers in a table on a notepad.
setup.caption: 3. Count how many of the 10 kinds lie on each marked part.

flow.do: 1. Fold the newspaper sheet in half four times, turning the sheet each time. Open it flat on a bed or a mat. The folds make 16 equal parts, in 4 rows of 4. 2. Draw a thick line down the middle fold. Write KEEP on the left half. It has 8 parts. 3. In the left half, draw a box around the top 4 parts. Write QUARTER. 4. Inside the quarter, draw a box around the top 2 parts. Write EIGHTH. 5. Write SIXTEENTH on the top left part. 6. Count the 10 kinds of pieces into the tumbler: 40, 20, 10, 6, 4, 3, 2, 2, 1 and 1.
flow.say: This sheet is a forest. Each kind of piece is one species. Rice is a common species with 40 members. The cardamom is a rare species with only 1.
flow.kid: Fold the sheet into 16 parts. Mark the half to keep. Mark the quarter, the eighth and the sixteenth. Count the 89 pieces into the tumbler.
flow.parent: A bed or a mat stops the pieces from bouncing. The boxes sit one inside the other, like a forest that is cut smaller and smaller. Mark them before any piece is scattered. That keeps the test fair.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Shrinking Forest Test. Here you fold a newspaper into 16 parts, mark which parts will be kept, and count out 10 kinds of pieces.

flow.do: 1. Explain that the right half of the forest will be cut down, and only the half marked KEEP will stay. 2. Ask how many of the 10 kinds will be found on the half. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Half the forest will be cut. How many of the 10 kinds will still be found on the half that stays? About 5, more than 5, or fewer than 5? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Half the forest will be cut. How many of the 10 kinds will be left? About 5, more or fewer? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: About 5, because half the forest should hold half the kinds. (A fair guess. The test will show.)
More than 5, because the rice and the dal will fall on both halves.

flow.context: This step of the Shrinking Forest Test is for guessing. You guess how many of the 10 kinds will be found on half the sheet, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Shake the tumbler to mix the pieces. 2. Hold the tumbler about 30 centimetres above the sheet. Pour slowly, and move your hand over every part of the sheet. 3. Pick up any piece that fell off the sheet. Drop it back on with your eyes closed. 4. Count how many of the 10 kinds lie on the half marked KEEP. 5. Count the kinds on the quarter, the eighth and the sixteenth. 6. Write the four numbers in the table. Write which kinds were missing from the half. 7. Collect all 89 pieces. Do the whole test 3 times.
flow.say: Scatter the pieces over the whole forest. Now the right half is cut down. Which of the 10 kinds can you still find on the left half? Which kinds are missing?
flow.kid: Mix the pieces. Pour them slowly all over the sheet. Count the kinds on the half. Count the kinds on the quarter, the eighth and the sixteenth. Write the numbers. Do it 3 times.

ask.q: Which kinds were missing from the half? What do they have in common?
good: The cardamom or the chilli, and sometimes the cloves or the peppercorns.
They are the kinds with only 1 or 2 pieces.

flow.parent: A kind counts if at least one piece of that kind lies on the part. A piece on a line belongs to the part that holds most of the piece. Expect about 8 kinds on the half, 6 on the quarter, 5 on the eighth and 3 on the sixteenth. Your numbers can be 1 or 2 more or less. If the pieces pile up in the middle, pour more slowly and move your hand wider.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Shrinking Forest Test. You scatter 89 pieces on the sheet 3 times. Each time you count how many of the 10 kinds lie on the half, the quarter, the eighth and the sixteenth.

flow.do: 1. For each part of the sheet, add the 3 numbers and divide by 3. 2. Make five bars: 10 for the whole sheet, then the four averages. Draw them, or build them from rows of rice grains. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 4. Ask which kinds went missing first, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Find the average for each part. Make five bars, drawn or built from grains. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Half the forest was cut. Why were more than half the kinds still there?
good: The common kinds fell on every part, so the half still had some of them.
Only the kinds with 1 or 2 pieces could all land on the half that was cut.

ask.q: Our pieces fell anywhere on the sheet. How is a real forest different?
good: Real plants and animals live where there is the right food, water or shade.
Some species live in only one corner of a forest.
Animals can move when the trees are cut, if there is somewhere to go.

check.q: In the Shrinking Forest Test, which kinds went missing first when the forest was cut?
options: The kinds with the most pieces
The kinds with only 1 or 2 pieces
The biggest pieces
check.why: A kind with 40 pieces lands on every part of the sheet, so some are always left. A kind with 1 piece is on the kept half only about half the time. Choosing the biggest pieces means looking at size. The test showed that the number of pieces mattered, and the size did not.

flow.context: This step of the Shrinking Forest Test works out the results. You find the average number of kinds on each part of the sheet, and explain which kinds went missing first.

flow.do: 1. Take the 6 chana in your hand. In the scatters, the 6 chana fell all over the sheet. Now they will be endemic: all 6 live in one part only. 2. Your child closes their eyes. Turn the sheet around once. Your child puts a finger down on the sheet. 3. Put all 6 chana on the part under the finger. Is that part in the half marked KEEP? Write yes or no. 4. Do this 6 times. Count how many times all 6 chana were lost.
flow.say: Now you change the test. The chana become an endemic species. All 6 live together in one part of the forest. What will happen to them when half the forest is cut?
flow.kid: Now all 6 chana live in one part. Close your eyes and choose the part. Is that part in the half you keep? Do this 6 times.

ask.q: There were 6 chana both times. Why were they lost more often this time?
good: When they were scattered, some always fell on the half we kept.
When all 6 lived in one part, cutting that part took all of them at once.

flow.parent: When the chana were scattered, at least one was on the kept half almost every time. With all 6 in one part, they are all lost about 3 times in 6. So the number of members is not the only thing that matters. How widely they are spread matters too.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Shrinking Forest Test. In the scatters, the 6 chana fell all over the sheet. Here all 6 are put in one part, like an endemic species, and you see how often they are all lost.

experiments.title: The Coin Years Test: can a small group die out by bad luck alone?
experiments.context: In this experiment you find out whether a small group of animals can die out by bad luck alone. Each coin is one adult animal. A toss decides whether she raises young. One group lives on a small island with room for 4 adults, and the other in a large forest with room for 16. Nobody hunts either group.
experiments.question: Two groups of animals follow the same rule. On average each adult leaves one young. One place has room for 4 adults and the other has room for 16. Does either group die out within 10 generations?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Nobody hunts these animals, and on average each adult leaves one young. Will the group of 4 still be alive after 10 generations? Will the group of 16? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Both groups use the same coins and the same rule. Only the room is different: 4 adults or 16. Run the small island 6 times and the large forest 2 times, because one run depends a lot on luck.
results_table: Number of adults after each generation, 1 to 10
Did the group die out? In which generation?

materials.item: coins of any kind. If you have fewer than 16, cut 16 squares of 2 centimetres from a carton and draw a dot on one side of each. The dot side is 'heads'.
a steel plate with a rim, or the lid of a box, to tip the coins onto
a steel tumbler to shake the coins in
paper and a pencil for the table

schedule.what: Learn the rule with 4 coins. Guess. Run the small island 6 times and the large forest 2 times. Explain the results. Then test two islands joined by a corridor.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all 8 runs. Count how many of the 6 small groups died out, and how many of the 2 large groups. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: adults after each generation
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Four coins tipped from a steel tumbler onto a steel plate, two showing heads and two showing tails.
setup.caption: 1. Each coin is one adult. Shake the coins and tip them onto the plate.

setup.art: A child's finger pointing at the two coins showing heads, with '2 heads, so 4 adults next' written on a notepad.
setup.caption: 2. Count the heads and double the number. That many adults live in the next generation.

setup.art: A notepad with two rows of numbers: a short row ending in 0 labelled 'room for 4', and a long row of ten numbers labelled 'room for 16'.
setup.caption: 3. Go on for 10 generations, or until no adult is left.

flow.do: 1. Put 4 coins in the tumbler. Each coin is one adult animal on a small island. 2. Shake the tumbler and tip the coins onto the plate. 3. A coin showing heads raised 2 young. A coin showing tails raised none. 4. Count the heads and double the number. That is the number of adults in the next generation. 5. The island has food for only 4 adults. If the number is more than 4, write 4. 6. Put that many coins back in the tumbler for the next toss.
flow.say: Each coin is one adult animal. Heads means she raised two young. Tails means she raised none. Then the old adults die, and the young become the new adults.
flow.kid: Each coin is one adult animal. Shake and tip the coins. Heads means two young. Tails means none. Count the heads and double them. The island fits only 4, so never write more than 4.
flow.parent: Half the coins land heads on average. So on average 4 adults leave 4 young, and the number should stay the same. Say this aloud, because the guess in the next step depends on it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Coin Years Test. Here you learn the rule with 4 coins. A coin showing heads is an adult who raised two young, and a coin showing tails raised none.

flow.do: 1. Explain the two places. The small island has room for 4 adults. The large forest has room for 16. 2. Ask whether each group will still be alive after 10 generations. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Nobody hunts these animals. On average each adult leaves one young. Will the group of 4 still be alive after 10 generations? Will the group of 16? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Nobody hunts these animals. Will the group of 4 last 10 generations? Will the group of 16? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Both will last, because births and deaths match on average. (A fair guess. The test will show.)
The small group might die out, because all 4 coins can land tails together.

flow.context: This step of the Coin Years Test is for guessing. You guess whether a group of 4 and a group of 16 will each last 10 generations, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Start with 4 coins. Toss, count the heads, double the number, and write it down. Never write more than 4. 2. Toss again with that many coins. 3. Stop after 10 generations, or when the number reaches 0. 4. Do 6 runs. For each run, write whether the group died out, and in which generation.
flow.say: This is the small island. Toss for each generation. If the number ever reaches zero, the group is gone, and nobody is left to have young.
flow.kid: Start with 4 coins. Toss and count the heads. Double them. Toss again with that many coins. Stop at 10 generations or at zero. Do 6 runs.
flow.parent: About 3 runs in every 4 end at zero before generation 10. So of your 6 runs, expect 4 or 5 to die out. If none do, that is unusual luck, and it is worth 3 more runs.
flow.context: This step of the Coin Years Test runs the small island. The island has room for 4 adults. You follow the group for up to 10 generations, 6 times over.

flow.do: 1. Now start with 16 coins. The large forest has room for 16 adults. 2. Toss, count the heads, double the number, and write it down. Never write more than 16. 3. Toss again with that many coins. 4. Stop after 10 generations, or at 0. 5. Do 2 runs.
flow.say: This is the large forest. The rule is the same. Only the room is different. Watch how low the number goes.
flow.kid: Now start with 16 coins. Toss and count the heads. Double them. Never write more than 16. Go on for 10 generations. Do 2 runs.

ask.q: What was the lowest number the large group reached?
good: It went down to 8 or 10 and came back up.
It never came near zero.

flow.parent: A group of 16 dies out within 10 generations only about 1 time in 8. If it happens to you, say so honestly and do one more run.
flow.context: This step of the Coin Years Test runs the large forest. The forest has room for 16 adults. The rule is the same as on the small island.

flow.do: 1. Count how many of the 6 small groups died out. Count how many of the 2 large groups died out. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Ask what could end a small group of real animals.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Count how many small groups died out. Count how many large groups died out. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Nobody hunted the small group. Why did they die out?
good: Sometimes all the coins landed tails, so no young were raised.
With only 2 or 4 animals, one bad toss can end the group.
With 16, some coins nearly always land heads.

ask.q: What could be a 'bad toss' for a real group of animals?
good: A year with no rain or little food.
A disease, a fire or a flood.
A year when few young are born, or all the young are male.

check.q: In the Coin Years Test, why did the group of 4 die out more often than the group of 16?
options: The group of 4 had a harder rule
With few coins, all can land tails together
The group of 16 had more food for each animal
check.why: Both groups had the same rule, so the test was fair. Four coins all land tails about 1 time in 16. Sixteen coins almost never do. Choosing the first answer means forgetting that only the room was different.

flow.context: This step of the Coin Years Test works out the results. You count how many groups of 4 and how many groups of 16 died out, and explain the difference.

flow.do: 1. Now run two small islands side by side, each with room for 4. Toss for island A, then for island B, for 10 generations. Both are gone only when both reach 0. 2. Run the pair once with no corridor. An island that reaches 0 stays empty. 3. Run the pair once with a corridor. If one island reaches 0 and the other has 2 or more, put 2 new coins on the empty island. They are young animals who walked across.
flow.say: Now you change the test. Two small islands are joined by a corridor of trees. When one island loses everyone, young animals from the other can walk across. Will that help? Why?
flow.kid: Run two islands of 4 side by side. First with no corridor. Then with a corridor. With a corridor, an empty island gets 2 new coins from the other.
flow.parent: One run each is too few to be sure, and that is worth saying aloud. On a computer, both islands were empty within 10 generations in about 11 tries out of 20 with no corridor. With the corridor it was about 4 tries out of 20. A corridor lets a lost group be replaced.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Coin Years Test. In the runs before, a group of 4 on one island usually died out. Here two islands of 4 are joined by a corridor, so one can refill the other.

experiments.title: The Bread Forest: is one big patch the same as sixteen small ones?
experiments.context: In this experiment a slice of bread is a damp forest. One slice stays whole and one is cut into 16 small squares. Both have the same amount of bread. You leave them under a fan and find out which dries faster, and where the drying starts.
experiments.question: One whole slice of bread and 16 small squares cut from another slice lie under the same fan. Which dries out faster? Which part of the whole slice dries first?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Both plates hold the same amount of bread. Will the whole slice or the 16 small squares dry faster, or will they dry the same? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Both slices come from the same loaf and are the same size and thickness. The crusts are cut off both. Both plates lie under the same fan for the same time. Only the cutting is different.
results_table: Whole slice: the middle feels (soft, leathery or hard)
Small squares: the middle of a square feels

materials.item: slices of soft, fresh bread from the same loaf
a knife, for the grown-up
plates or one large tray
a ruler with millimetres
a ceiling fan or a table fan, and a clock

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. Wash your hands before touching the bread, so that the dry bread can still be eaten afterwards.

schedule.what: Cut the bread and lay out both plates (11 minutes). Check after 1, 2 and 3 hours (6 minutes in all). Break the pieces, measure the dry rim and explain (8 minutes).

experiments.record: Fill in the table at 1, 2 and 3 hours. Write the width of the hard rim on the whole slice in millimetres. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

setup.art: Two slices of white bread with the crusts cut off: one whole on a plate, the other cut into 16 small squares spread out on a second plate with gaps between them.
setup.caption: 1. Keep one slice whole. Cut the other into 16 squares and spread them out.

setup.art: The two plates side by side on a table under a spinning ceiling fan, with a clock on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Leave both plates under the same fan. Check every hour.

setup.art: The whole slice broken in two, showing a pale hard rim around a soft middle, with a ruler measuring the width of the rim.
setup.caption: 3. After 3 hours, break the whole slice and measure the hard rim.

flow.do: 1. Cut the crusts off both slices, so that all four sides are soft. 2. Put one slice whole on a plate. 3. Cut the other slice 3 times each way, to make 16 small squares. 4. Spread the squares on the second plate, with a gap of about 2 centimetres between them. 5. Put both plates under the fan. Write down the time.
flow.say: The whole slice is one big forest. The 16 squares are 16 small forests. Together they have the same amount of bread as the big one.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the bread. Keep one slice whole. Cut the other into 16 squares. Spread the squares out. Put both plates under the fan.
flow.parent: Use the softest, freshest bread you have. If you have no bread, use 2 idlis of the same size. Keep one whole and cut the other into 8 pieces.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bread Forest. Here a grown-up cuts one slice of bread into 16 small squares and leaves another slice whole.

flow.do: 1. Ask which will dry faster, the whole slice or the 16 squares, or whether they will dry the same. 2. Ask for the reason. 3. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Both plates have the same amount of bread and the same fan. Which will dry faster? Or will they dry the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which will dry faster, the whole slice or the 16 squares? Or the same? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The same, because it is the same amount of bread. (A fair guess. The test will show.)
The squares, because the air can reach more sides.

flow.context: This step of the Bread Forest is for guessing. You guess whether a whole slice of bread or 16 small squares will dry faster under a fan, and say why.
