flow.do: 1. After 1 hour, press the middle of the whole slice gently with a clean finger. Then press its rim. 2. Press the middle of three small squares. 3. Write soft, leathery or hard for each. 4. Do the same after 2 hours and after 3 hours.
flow.say: Press gently. Is the middle of the big slice soft, leathery or hard? What about the rim? What about the middle of a small square?
flow.kid: Press the middle of the whole slice. Press the rim. Press three small squares. Write soft, leathery or hard. Do this each hour.
flow.wait: Check after 1 hour, 2 hours and 3 hours
flow.parent: On a dry day, the small squares are hard in 2 to 3 hours. The whole slice gets a hard rim but stays bendy in the middle. On a damp monsoon day everything is slower. Then leave both plates under the fan for 5 or 6 hours, or overnight.
flow.context: This step of the Bread Forest checks the bread each hour. You press the whole slice and the small squares, and write how dry each one feels.

flow.do: 1. After 3 hours, break the whole slice across the middle. Look at the broken side. 2. Measure how far the hard, dry part reaches in from the rim, in millimetres. 3. Break two small squares. Is any soft part left inside? 4. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Break the whole slice in the middle. Measure the hard rim. Break two small squares. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Where did the whole slice dry first? Why there?
good: At the rim, because the moving air reaches the sides as well as the top.
The middle is far from any side.

ask.q: A forest edge is hotter, drier and windier than the middle. Which keeps more damp, shady forest: one big patch or 16 small ones?
good: One big patch, because the middle is far from the edge.
A small patch is all edge, like the small squares that dried right through.

check.q: In the Bread Forest, why did the 16 small squares dry right through before the whole slice did?
options: They had less bread in total
Every part of a small square is near a cut side
The fan blew harder on their plate
check.why: Both plates had the same amount of bread and the same fan. Cutting made many new sides, and air dries bread from the sides as well as the top. In a small square no part is far from a side. Choosing the first answer means forgetting that the 16 squares were one whole slice.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Bread Forest. You break the whole slice and two small squares, measure how far the drying reached in, and explain the difference.

activities.title: Ten Minutes at the Window: how many kinds, and how many of each?
activities.context: This short activity starts the unit. You will find out how much life is in one small place. You watch one place for 10 minutes and count how many kinds of living beings you see, and how many of each kind.

materials.item: a pencil and a sheet of paper
a clock or a phone timer
a window, a balcony, a doorstep or a potted plant

activities.record: Keep the table. Write how many kinds you saw, how many beings in all, and how many kinds you saw only once.

setup.art: A child sitting at a window with a notepad, watching a crow on a wire, a squirrel on a tree and ants on the sill.
setup.caption: 1. Sit at a window or a doorstep and watch for 10 minutes.

setup.art: A table with three columns, Kind, Tally and Total, filled with tally marks for crow, ant, pigeon and neem tree.
setup.caption: 2. Write each kind once. Add a tally mark every time you see her.

flow.do: 1. Choose a spot with a view of the outdoors, such as a window, a balcony or a doorstep. 2. Rule a table with three columns: Kind, Tally and Total. 3. Set a timer for 10 minutes.
flow.say: We will count the living beings we can see from one spot. Plants count too. Each different kind goes in the table once.
flow.kid: Choose a spot. Draw a table with Kind, Tally and Total. Set a timer for 10 minutes.
flow.parent: If you see nothing at first, look at one potted plant or one tree for the whole time. Ants, flies, crows, pigeons, squirrels, bees, weeds in cracks and tiny insects on leaves all count. A kind can be a plain description, such as 'small brown bird'.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ten Minutes at the Window. Here you choose a spot and set up a table.

flow.do: 1. Watch for 10 minutes. 2. When you see a living being, write her kind in the table. Use a description if you do not know the name. 3. Add a tally mark each time you see another one of that kind. 4. Count plants too, such as a neem tree, a pot of tulsi and weeds.
flow.say: Look slowly. What kinds can you see? Write each kind once. Make a tally mark each time you see one more.
flow.kid: Watch for 10 minutes. Write each kind once. Add a tally mark each time you see her again.
flow.parent: Do not help with names. Counting 'two kinds of ant' or 'black bird' is fine.
flow.context: This step of Ten Minutes at the Window is the counting. You watch one place and tally each kind of living being.

flow.do: 1. Add up each row. 2. Count the kinds, and count all the beings. 3. Count the kinds seen only once. 4. Ask what these kinds tell you.
flow.say: How many kinds did you find? How many beings in all? How many kinds did you see only once?
flow.kid: Add the tallies. Count the kinds. Count the kinds seen only once.

ask.q: If you watched again tomorrow, which kinds would you probably see again?
good: The ones with the most tallies, such as crows or ants.
The kinds seen only once might not come back, so they were harder to find.

ask.q: A scientist counting species in a forest cannot see everything either. What could she miss?
good: Shy or rare kinds who were not there in that hour.
Kinds who come out only at night.

flow.context: This is the last step of Ten Minutes at the Window. You count the kinds and the beings, and find the kinds you saw only once.

activities.title: Same Count, Different Forest: why counting kinds is not enough
activities.context: In this activity you find out why counting kinds can fool you. Two bowls are two forests. Both have 10 kinds of kitchen pieces, but one has an even mix and the other has one kind with almost all the pieces. You take a sample from each and count the kinds you find.
activities.question: Two forests both have 10 species. In one, every species has 4 members. In the other, one species has 31 and each of the other nine has 1. Which forest shows more species in a small sample?

materials.item: ten kinds of dry pieces, such as rice, toor dal, masoor dal, moong, chana, rajma, urad, groundnut, peppercorn and dry chilli. You need 35 rice and 5 of each of the other nine kinds.
two bowls
paper and a pencil for the table

activities.record: Keep the table of kinds found in each sample. Write the average for each bowl.

setup.art: Two bowls side by side. The left bowl holds a mix of ten kinds in small equal piles. The right bowl is full of rice with nine other pieces scattered in it.
setup.caption: 1. Make Forest A with 4 of each kind. Make Forest B with mostly rice.

setup.art: A child with eyes closed taking one piece at a time from a bowl and laying the pieces in a row on a plate.
setup.caption: 2. With your eyes closed, take 8 pieces from a bowl.

setup.art: A plate with 8 pieces sorted into small groups by kind, and a table beside it with the number of kinds written.
setup.caption: 3. Sort the 8 pieces and count the kinds.

flow.do: 1. Make Forest A in one bowl: 4 pieces of each of the 10 kinds, which is 40 pieces. 2. Make Forest B in the other bowl: 31 rice and 1 piece of each of the other 9 kinds, which is 40 pieces. 3. Check that both bowls hold 10 kinds and 40 pieces.
flow.say: Both bowls are forests with 10 species and 40 members. The only difference is how the members are shared out.
flow.kid: Fill bowl A with 4 pieces of each kind. Fill bowl B with 31 rice and 1 of each other kind.
flow.parent: Counting 40 pieces twice is quick if you sort them in small piles first. Any ten kinds work, as long as bowl B has 31 of one kind and 1 of each of the nine others.
flow.context: This is the first step of Same Count, Different Forest. Here you make two forests with the same number of kinds, shared out differently.

flow.do: 1. Ask which bowl will show more kinds in a sample of 8 pieces. 2. Ask for the reason. 3. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Both forests have 10 species. You will take 8 pieces from each, with your eyes closed. Which forest will show more kinds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Both bowls have 10 kinds. You take 8 pieces from each. Which shows more kinds?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The same, because both have 10 kinds. (A fair guess. The test will show.)
Bowl A, because the pieces are shared out evenly.
Bowl B, because it has more rice to pick.

flow.context: This step of Same Count, Different Forest is for guessing. You guess which bowl will show more kinds in a sample, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Stir bowl A. With your eyes closed, take 8 pieces one at a time. 2. Lay them out and count the kinds. Write the number in a table (bowl, try, kinds). 3. Put the pieces back and stir. 4. Do this 3 times for bowl A and 3 times for bowl B.
flow.say: Stir the bowl. Close your eyes. Take 8 pieces, one at a time. Now count how many kinds you got.
flow.kid: Stir the bowl. Close your eyes. Take 8 pieces. Count the kinds. Do this 3 times for each bowl.
flow.parent: Expect about 6 kinds from bowl A, between 5 and 7. Expect about 3 kinds from bowl B, between 2 and 4. If the two bowls give the same number, mix the bowls better and check that bowl B really holds 31 of one kind.
flow.context: This step of Same Count, Different Forest is the sampling. You take 8 pieces from each forest, 3 times, and count the kinds.

flow.do: 1. Find the average number of kinds for each bowl. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Ask which forest has more rare species, and which forest a scientist would find easier to measure.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Find the average for each bowl. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Both bowls have 10 kinds. Why did bowl B show fewer in a sample?
good: Most pieces in bowl B were rice, so the sample was mostly rice.
The nine rare kinds had only 1 piece each, so they were easy to miss.

ask.q: Which forest would you protect first? Why?
good: Forest B, because 9 of its species have only 1 member each.
Forest B, because losing the rice kind would leave only one member of each of the others.

check.q: Two forests both have 10 species. What does that count leave out?
options: How many members each species has
Which forest is bigger
Which forest has more trees
check.why: The bowls both had 10 kinds, but one was even and one was almost all rice. The number of kinds does not show how many members each kind has, so it hides which kinds are rare. The other two answers are about size, and the bowls were the same size.

flow.context: This is the last step of Same Count, Different Forest. You find the average number of kinds in each sample, and explain the difference.

activities.title: Only Here: where in India do some species live?
activities.context: In this activity you mark on a map of India the only places where some living beings are found. Then you look for what these places have in common.

materials.item: a map of India from an atlas or a school book, or a sheet of paper to draw a rough outline on
a pencil and a colour pencil
a ruler

activities.record: Keep the map with its dots and names. Write one sentence on what these places have in common.

setup.art: A map of India with five coloured dots: Gujarat, the Western Ghats strip, the Andaman Sea, Manipur and the Nicobar Islands.
setup.caption: 1. Find each place on the map and put a dot.

setup.art: The same map with a species name written beside each dot and the Western Ghats strip shaded.
setup.caption: 2. Write the species who live only in that place.

flow.do: 1. Open the atlas to the map of India. 2. If you have no atlas, draw a rough outline of India on a sheet of paper. Make it wide at the top and narrowing to a point at the bottom. 3. Find the Western Ghats. They are the hills along the west coast, from Gujarat to the tip of Tamil Nadu. 4. Find the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the sea to the east.
flow.say: Some living beings are found naturally in only one place in the world. Scientists call them endemic. Let us find some of those places.
flow.kid: Open a map of India. Find the hills along the west coast. Find the islands in the east sea.
flow.parent: You do not need a perfect map. A rough outline is enough. Gujarat is the western bulge, Manipur is in the far northeast, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie out in the sea to the southeast.
flow.context: This is the first step of Only Here. Here you find the places on a map of India where some species live and nowhere else.

flow.do: 1. Put a dot at each of these places and write the species beside it. 2. Gir forest in Gujarat: the Asiatic lion. 3. Western Ghats: the lion-tailed macaque, the Nilgiri tahr and the purple frog. 4. An island called Narcondam in the Andaman Sea: the Narcondam hornbill. 5. Nicobar Islands: the Nicobar megapode. 6. Loktak lake in Manipur: the sangai deer.
flow.say: Put a dot at each place. Write the name of the species beside it. Today these species are found only in these places.
flow.kid: Put a dot at each place. Gir forest in Gujarat: the Asiatic lion. Western Ghats: lion-tailed macaque, Nilgiri tahr, purple frog. Narcondam island: the Narcondam hornbill. Nicobar Islands: the Nicobar megapode. Loktak lake in Manipur: the sangai deer.
flow.parent: The lion is now found only in and around Gir. The Nilgiri tahr is a wild goat of high grassy cliffs. The purple frog lives underground for most of the year. The Narcondam hornbill lives on an island of about 7 square kilometres. The sangai is a deer who walks on floating mats of grass in Loktak lake.
flow.context: This step of Only Here puts the species on the map. You mark five places and write who lives only there.

flow.do: 1. Count how many species you marked in each place. 2. Find the place with the smallest area. 3. Ask what these places have in common. 4. Ask which species would suffer most if one fire or disease swept through its place.
flow.say: Which place has the most species on your list? Which place is the smallest?
flow.kid: Count the species at each dot. Find the smallest place.

ask.q: What do an island, a lake, a hill range and one forest have in common?
good: Each one is cut off from other places like it.
Beings who live there cannot easily move to another place.
Each one has a small area.

ask.q: Which species on your map has the smallest range? Why is she at greater risk?
good: The Narcondam hornbill, because her whole range is one small island.
One storm or one disease on the island could reach every bird.

flow.context: This is the last step of Only Here. You compare the places on your map and look for what they share.

activities.title: The Cold Hilltop: what happens to a mountain species when the air warms?
activities.context: In this activity a paper triangle is a hill. A cold-loving frog lives only near the top, where the air is cool. You find out how much of her home is left when the air warms and the cool zone moves up.
activities.question: A cold-loving frog lives only on the top part of a hill. The air warms, and the cool zone moves up. How much smaller does her home become?

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper, A4 or larger
a ruler with centimetres
a pencil and a colour pencil

activities.record: Keep the hill drawing with both lines. Write the area above each line and the share of the whole hill.

setup.art: A paper triangle hill 20 centimetres wide and 10 centimetres high, with a horizontal line 6 centimetres up and the top shaded green.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the hill. Shade the cool zone above the first line.

setup.art: The same hill with a second line 8 centimetres up and a smaller top shaded in a darker green.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the second line. This is where the cool zone is after the air warms.

setup.art: A second, lower hill 7 centimetres high with a dotted line at 8 centimetres floating in the air above it.
setup.caption: 3. On a lower hill, the cool zone has no land at all.

flow.do: 1. On the paper, draw a straight line 20 centimetres long near the bottom. 2. Mark its middle at 10 centimetres. 3. Mark a point 10 centimetres straight above the middle. 4. Join the point to both ends of the line. This is a hill, 20 centimetres wide and 10 centimetres high. 5. Write: 1 centimetre of height stands for 200 metres.
flow.say: Draw a hill as a triangle. It is 20 centimetres wide and 10 centimetres high. Each centimetre of height stands for 200 metres, so the hill is 2,000 metres high.
flow.kid: Draw a base line 20 centimetres long. Mark a point 10 centimetres above the middle. Join it to both ends.
flow.parent: The air gets colder by about 6 degrees for every 1,000 metres you climb. So the top of this hill is about 12 degrees cooler than the bottom.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cold Hilltop. Here you draw a hill as a paper triangle.

flow.do: 1. A cold-loving frog lives only above 1,200 metres. That is 6 centimetres up. 2. Draw a line across the hill 6 centimetres above the base line. 3. Shade the part of the hill above the line. This is the frog's home. 4. Now the air warms by 2 to 3 degrees. The cool zone moves up by about 400 metres, which is 2 centimetres. 5. Draw a second line 8 centimetres up. Use another colour.
flow.say: The frog needs cool air, so she lives only above this line. When the air warms, the cool zone moves up to the second line.
flow.kid: Draw a line 6 centimetres up. Shade above it. Draw a second line 8 centimetres up.
flow.parent: Warming of 2 to 3 degrees moves a cool zone up by about 300 to 500 metres. We use 400 metres, which is 2 centimetres on the drawing.
flow.context: This step of the Cold Hilltop marks the frog's home. The first line is her home now. The second line is her home after the air warms.

flow.do: 1. Ask how much smaller the frog's home will be when the cool zone moves up: a little, half, or a lot. 2. Ask for the reason. 3. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: The cool zone moves up by only 2 centimetres. How much smaller will the frog's home be: a little, about half, or a lot? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The cool zone moves up 2 centimetres. How much smaller is her home? A little, half or a lot?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: A little, because 2 centimetres is not much. (A fair guess. The drawing will show.)
A lot, because the hill gets narrow near the top.

flow.context: This step of the Cold Hilltop is for guessing. You guess how much smaller the frog's home becomes, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Measure the width of the hill along the first line. 2. The height of that top triangle is 4 centimetres. Find its area: width times height, divided by 2. 3. Measure the width along the second line, and find its area in the same way. 4. The whole hill has an area of 100 square centimetres. Find the share of the hill for each line.
flow.say: Measure the width along each line. The area of a triangle is width times height, divided by 2. How much of the hill is left in each top?
flow.kid: Measure the width at each line. Find each area. Write the share of the whole hill.
flow.parent: The first line gives a triangle 8 centimetres wide and 4 centimetres high, so 8 x 4 ÷ 2 = 16 square centimetres, which is 16 in every 100 of the hill. The second line gives a triangle 4 centimetres wide and 2 centimetres high, so 4 x 2 ÷ 2 = 4 square centimetres, which is 4 in every 100. A move of 2 centimetres cut the home to one quarter of its size.
flow.context: This step of the Cold Hilltop measures the frog's home. You find the area above each line and compare it with the whole hill.

flow.do: 1. Now make a lower hill. Cover the top of your hill with a sheet of paper, so only the part below 7 centimetres shows. 2. The second line is 8 centimetres up. It is now in the air above the lower hill. 3. Ask where the frog can live on this hill after the air warms. 4. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: On this lower hill, the cool zone has moved above the top of the hill. Where can the frog live now? Tell me what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Cover the top of your hill so only 7 centimetres show. Is the second line on the hill? Where can the frog live now?

ask.q: The cool zone moved up by one fifth of the hill's height, but the frog's home became one quarter as big. Why?
good: A hill gets narrower towards the top, so each step up has less land.
The top part of a hill is a small triangle.

ask.q: Where could the frog go if the nearest higher hill is far away?
good: Nowhere. She cannot cross the warm valley.
She might live on if another hill is near, which is why corridors and higher ground matter.

check.q: A cold-loving species lives only above 1,200 metres. The cool zone moves up 400 metres, and the hill is 1,400 metres high. What is left?
options: Her whole home
Half of her home
No home at all
check.why: The cool zone now starts at 1,600 metres, and the hill ends at 1,400 metres. There is no land above the line. Choosing half means treating the move as a small shift, when it moved the zone off the top of the hill.

flow.parent: A real hill is not a triangle, and animals and plants can sometimes adapt or move to another hill. The drawing shows why a steep, narrow top has the most to lose.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Cold Hilltop. You test a lower hill, and explain what happens to a species whose home moves higher than the hill.

activities.title: Five Causes: sort ten real cases
activities.context: In this activity you sort ten real cases into the five main causes of species loss today. Then you count which cause comes up most.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Keep the sorted sheet with the five headings and the letters of the cases.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with five columns headed Habitat loss, Taking too many, Brought-in species, Pollution and Warming, with letters written under each.
setup.caption: 1. Write the five causes as headings.

setup.art: A child reading a list of cases and writing the letter of each case under a heading.
setup.caption: 2. Write the letter of each case under its cause.

flow.do: 1. Draw five columns on the paper, or put out five bowls or sheets. 2. Write these headings: Habitat loss, Taking too many, Brought-in species, Pollution, and Warming. 3. Read the meaning of each aloud. Habitat loss means a place is cleared or cut up. Taking too many means too many are hunted, fished or collected. A brought-in species is carried by people to a new place. Pollution is poison or dirt in the air, water or soil. Warming is a changing climate.
flow.say: Species are in danger today for five main reasons. We will sort ten real cases into them.
flow.kid: Draw five columns, or set out five bowls. Write the five headings. Read what each one means.
flow.context: This is the first step of Five Causes. Here you set up five columns for the five main causes of species loss.

flow.do: 1. Read cases A to E, one at a time. 2. Write the letter of each case under the cause that fits best. 3. A. A grassland is ploughed for farms. B. Tigers are shot for their skins. C. Rats come off ships and eat birds' eggs on an island. D. A cattle medicine poisons vultures who eat the dead cattle. E. The sea warms and corals turn white.
flow.say: Read each case. Which cause does it show? Write its letter under that heading.
flow.kid: A: a grassland is ploughed for farms. B: tigers are shot for their skins. C: rats from ships eat island birds' eggs. D: a cattle medicine poisons vultures. E: the sea warms and corals turn white. Write each letter under its cause.
flow.parent: Answers. A: habitat loss. B: taking too many. C: brought-in species. D: pollution. E: warming.
flow.context: This step of Five Causes is the first half of the sorting. You read cases A to E and put each one under its cause.

flow.do: 1. Read cases F to J. 2. Write the letter of each case under the cause that fits best. 3. F. A new highway cuts a forest in two. G. Pangolins are caught for their scales. H. Turtles eat plastic bags in the sea. I. A garden shrub spreads through a forest and shades out the grass. J. Mountain plants move higher as the air warms.
flow.say: Now cases F to J. Which cause does each one show? A case can fit two causes, so choose the one that fits best.
flow.kid: F: a new highway cuts a forest in two. G: pangolins are caught for their scales. H: turtles eat plastic bags. I: a garden shrub spreads through a forest. J: mountain plants move higher as the air warms.
flow.parent: Answers. F: habitat loss. G: taking too many. H: pollution. I: brought-in species. J: warming. Case F also kills animals who are hit by vehicles, so a case can show two causes.
flow.context: This step of Five Causes is the second half of the sorting. You read cases F to J and put each one under its cause.

flow.do: 1. Count the cases under each heading. 2. Ask which cases could fit two causes. 3. Ask which cause your child thinks is hardest to stop.
flow.say: How many cases are under each heading? Could any case fit under two? Which cause is hardest to stop, and why?
flow.kid: Count the cases under each heading. Could any case fit two causes? Which cause is hardest to stop?

ask.q: Some real species suffer from two causes at once. Why is that worse?
good: One cause weakens her and the second finishes the job.
Fixing one cause is not enough.

flow.context: This is the last step of Five Causes. You count the cases under each cause and say which cases could fit two.

activities.title: The Village Meeting: should people live inside a protected forest?
activities.context: This is a role-play about a real argument. You will find out why sensible people disagree about it. A forest has been made a protected area, and a village lives inside it. Three speakers each give their view, and then you decide what you think.

materials.item: three role cards written on paper
a pencil and paper
a timer or a clock

activities.record: Keep your written decision: your view, the evidence, and what you still want to know.

setup.art: Three role cards on a table: a forest biologist, a herder from the forest, and a forest officer.
setup.caption: 1. Write the three role cards.

setup.art: Three people sitting in a circle, each speaking in turn while the others listen, with a timer in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Each speaker talks for 1 minute. Then each asks one question.

flow.do: 1. Write three role cards. 2. The wildlife biologist: 'Tigers and deer need land with no cattle, no roads and no villages. In some reserves, wildlife increased after villages moved out of the core.' 3. The herder from the forest: 'My family has lived here for generations. We guard this forest, and the forest feeds our cattle. Moving us out is unfair.' 4. The forest officer: 'The law protects wildlife, and a 2006 law also gives forest peoples the right to stay and care for their land. I must find a way that follows both.' 5. Give one role to each player. If you are alone, you play all three.
flow.say: A forest is a protected area, and a village lives inside it. There are three speakers. Each one has a real view that people hold in India.
flow.kid: Write three cards. The biologist says: tigers and deer need land with no people. The herder says: my family guards this forest. The officer says: the law must protect both. Give one role to each player.
flow.parent: Each view is real. Many wildlife biologists want core areas with no people. Many forest peoples and social scientists say forest people are the best guards. The Forest Rights Act of 2006 gives forest peoples rights to forest land. Scientists and communities still argue about the best answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Village Meeting. Here you write three role cards for a real argument about protected forests.

flow.do: 1. Each speaker talks for 1 minute and gives the best reason for their view. 2. Each speaker then asks one question of one other speaker. 3. Each speaker says one thing the other views have right. 4. If you are alone, write what each speaker says.
flow.say: Each speaker has one minute. Give your best reason. Then ask one question. Then say one thing another speaker has right.
flow.kid: Speak for 1 minute with your best reason. Ask one question. Say one thing another speaker has right.
flow.parent: Leave the winner for later. Keep your child to the speaker's role, even when they disagree with it. The skill is to state a view fairly.
flow.context: This step of the Village Meeting is the meeting itself. Each speaker gives a reason, asks a question, and names a point the others have right.

flow.do: 1. Everyone steps out of their role. 2. Each person writes what they think: which plan they would choose for one forest, and why. 3. They write one piece of evidence they would want before deciding. 4. They say what they thought would happen in the meeting, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Step out of your role. Which plan would you choose for one forest? What evidence would you want first? Tell me what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Step out of your role. Say or write which plan you would choose. Say or write what evidence you want first.

ask.q: What would you want to know about this one forest before you decide?
good: How many animals live there now, and how many lived there before.
Whether the village has damaged the forest or looked after it.
Whether wild animals and the villagers can live apart without being harmed.

flow.parent: There is no single right answer, and scientists disagree. A strong answer uses evidence and says what is still unknown.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Village Meeting. You step out of your role and write your own view, with the evidence you would want.

projects.title: A Rescue Plan: one Indian species and how to keep her alive
projects.context: In this four-day project you choose one Indian species who is at risk. You find out where she lives and what threatens her, and then you write a rescue plan that you could explain to a village meeting.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a sheet of paper for the map
colour pencils
a book about Indian wildlife, or the internet with a grown-up (the Red List and the India Biodiversity Portal have pages on many species)

schedule.what: Choose a species. Find where she lives, how many are left and her step on the Red List.
Find what threatens her. Sort the threats under the five causes.
Draw her range on a map. Choose three actions for the plan.
Write the plan on one page, with what nobody knows yet. Read it aloud.

projects.record: Keep the fact page, the map and the one-page plan. The plan lists three actions, who must agree to each, and one thing nobody knows yet.

setup.art: A child at a table with a notebook, an open wildlife book and a photograph of a Nilgiri tahr, writing facts in a list.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one species. Write where she lives, how many are left and her Red List step.

setup.art: A sheet with a hand-drawn map of a mountain range, the species' range shaded, and three numbered actions written beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Draw her range. Write a plan with three actions.

flow.do: 1. Choose one species from the list in the parent note, or one of your own. 2. Write where she lives, how many are left and her step on the Red List. 3. Look in a book or online with a grown-up. 4. Put a question mark beside any fact you are not sure of.
flow.say: Which species shall we try to rescue? Where does she live? How many are left? What step of the Red List is she on?
flow.kid: Choose one species who is at risk. Find where she lives. Find how many are left. Find her Red List step.
flow.parent: Ready choices, with facts. Great Indian bustard: a big bird of dry grassland in Rajasthan and Gujarat, Critically Endangered, about 130 left, hurt by lost grassland and power lines. Nilgiri tahr: a wild goat of high grassy cliffs in the Western Ghats, Endangered, a few thousand left. Sangai: a deer who walks on floating mats of grass in Loktak lake, Manipur, Endangered, a few hundred left. Gharial: a fish-eating crocodile of clear northern rivers, Critically Endangered, hurt by dams, sand mining and fishing nets. Lion-tailed macaque: a monkey of Western Ghats rainforest, Endangered, a few thousand left.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rescue Plan. Here you choose one Indian species at risk and find the basic facts about her.

flow.do: 1. For your species, write every threat you can find. 2. Sort the threats under the five causes: habitat loss, taking too many, brought-in species, pollution and warming. 3. Ask which cause is the biggest, and how you know. 4. Write what protects her now, such as a park, a sanctuary or a law.
flow.say: What threatens her? Which of the five causes does each threat belong to? What protects her already?
flow.kid: Write every threat to her. Sort them under the five causes. Write what protects her now.
flow.parent: Most species face two or three causes together. If a threat fits no cause, write it down anyway and ask why.
flow.context: This step of the Rescue Plan finds the threats to your species and sorts them under the five main causes of species loss.

flow.do: 1. Mark her range on the map with a colour pencil, or list the places where she lives. 2. Mark any protected area inside it. 3. Write three actions for the plan. For example: make her protected area larger, join two areas with a corridor, start a second group in another place, or reduce one threat. 4. For each action write who must agree. Think of villagers, farmers, officials and visitors.
flow.say: Show where she lives on the map. Now choose three actions that would help her most. Who would need to agree to each one?
flow.kid: Mark her range on the map, or list the places. Choose three actions. Write who must agree to each action.

ask.q: Which action helps if one fire or one disease reaches her whole range?
good: A second group in another place.
A corridor that lets her move or be replaced.

flow.context: This step of the Rescue Plan draws the range of your species and chooses three actions to help her.

flow.do: 1. Write the plan on one page: the species, the three actions and the reason for each. 2. Write one thing that nobody knows yet about her or about the plan. 3. Read the plan aloud to a family member. 4. Ask your child to say what they thought would be hardest, what they found, and why.
flow.say: Read your plan to someone at home. Say what you think will be hardest. What does nobody know yet?
flow.kid: Write the plan on one page. Write one thing nobody knows yet. Read the plan aloud.

ask.q: What would you want to find out before starting your plan?
good: How many are left now, and whether the number is rising or falling.
Whether people living nearby agree with the plan.
Whether the actions have worked for other species.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Rescue Plan. You write a one-page plan with three actions, and say honestly what nobody knows yet.

challenges.title: A Way Through: join two forests with one strip of trees
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Coin Years Test, a corridor between two small islands lowered the risk of losing everybody. Here you plan a corridor between two forests on a map, at the lowest cost.
challenges.problem: Plan a strip of trees from Forest A to Forest B. The strip may cost at most 8 points. Find the cheapest strip, and find the squares that would hurt the plan most if one became a village.
constraints: The strip moves from square to square, up, down, left or right. It does not move diagonally.
A field costs 3 points, scrub costs 1, a road costs 2 for an underpass, and a river costs 2 for a bridge.
A village square cannot be used. Forest squares cost nothing.
materials: graph paper or a ruler and plain paper
general: Follow the scrub squares, because each costs only 1.
Cross the road once, at the square where the underpass is cheapest.
Avoid fields, because one field costs as much as three scrub squares.
creative: Take a longer way round, if it avoids all fields and costs less.
Cross the road in a place where the squares on both sides are scrub.
Find two different strips with the same cost. A second route is a spare if one is blocked.
challenges.your_turn: Now change one square of the map. Turn a scrub square in row 5 into a village. Find the new cheapest cost. Which squares, if one became a village, would push the cost above 8?

setup.art: A grid map of 7 columns and 6 rows with forest on the left and right edges, fields, scrub, a road, a river and a village in between.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the map onto graph paper.

setup.art: The same map with a coloured line of squares joining the left forest to the right forest, and the cost written under each square.
setup.caption: 2. Colour a strip from Forest A to Forest B. Add up its cost.

flow.do: 1. Draw a grid of 7 columns and 6 rows, with squares 2 centimetres wide. 2. Fill the squares from the rows below. A is Forest A and B is Forest B. The letter f is a field and S is scrub. R is a road, W is a river and V is a village. 3. Row 1: A f f f S S B. 4. Row 2: A f V V S W B. 5. Row 3: A S S V S W B. 6. Row 4: A S R R R R B. 7. Row 5: A f S S S S B. 8. Row 6: A f f V S S B. 9. Costs: a field costs 3, scrub 1, a road 2 and a river 2. A village cannot be used.
flow.say: Here is a map of two forests with fields, scrub, a road, a river and a village between them. Draw it. Each square costs points to turn into trees: field 3, scrub 1, road 2, river 2. A village cannot be used.
flow.kid: Draw a grid with 7 columns and 6 rows. Copy the rows from your grown-up. A is the left forest. B is the right forest. Costs: field 3, scrub 1, road 2, river 2. No village.
flow.parent: Costs. A field is 3, scrub is 1, a road is 2 for an underpass, a river is 2 for a bridge. A village cannot be crossed. Forest squares are free.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Way Through. Here you copy a map with two forests and the land between them.

flow.do: 1. Colour a strip of squares, or lay a string along them. It runs from Forest A to Forest B. 2. Move up, down, left or right. 3. Write the cost of each square under it. 4. Add up the total. 5. Is it 8 or less? 6. Try to find a cheaper strip.
flow.say: Colour a strip from one forest to the other. Add up its cost. Can you find one that costs less?
flow.kid: Colour a strip, or lay a string, from forest A to forest B. Add up the cost. Look for a cheaper strip.
flow.parent: The cheapest strip costs 7. There are two routes that cost 7. One goes through row 4 and crosses one road square, then follows the scrub squares of row 5. The other goes along row 5, with one field square at the start, and then four scrub squares.
flow.context: This step of A Way Through finds a strip that joins the forests and costs 8 points or less.

flow.do: 1. Pick one scrub square on your cheapest strip. 2. Turn that square into a village, and find the new cheapest cost. 3. Try another scrub square. 4. Find which squares, if one became a village, would push the cheapest cost above 8. 5. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Now a new village is built on one square. Does the cheapest strip cost more? Which squares would hurt the plan most?
flow.kid: Turn one scrub square into a village. Find the new cheapest cost. Which squares hurt the plan most?
flow.parent: Two squares in row 5 raise the cheapest cost to 9. They are the squares in columns 4 and 5, which are the second and third scrub squares from the left. Every cheap route passes through both of them, so protecting those squares matters more than protecting any other scrub square. Real planners look for these narrow points on a map.

ask.q: Why does one square on a corridor matter so much?
good: A strip is only as strong as its narrowest point.
If one square is lost, the animals cannot pass, and the two forests are cut apart again.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Way Through. You test what happens when one square of the strip becomes a village, and find the squares that matter most.

challenges.title: Keep the Last Four Alive: choose a plan with coins
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Coin Years Test, a group of 4 coins often died out. Here the last 4 birds of a species live on one small island, and you have 6 points to spend on a plan to keep them alive.
challenges.problem: Choose a plan that costs 6 points or less. Test it with coins and find out how often the birds die out within 10 generations. Compare it with the other plans.
constraints: Plan A costs 0. Nothing changes. The birds stay on one island with room for 4.
Plan B costs 6. Bring 4 more birds from a zoo, and make the island bigger, with room for 8. Start with 8 coins.
Plan C costs 3. Make a second island with room for 4, and move 2 birds there. There is no corridor.
Plan D costs 5. Make a second island with room for 4, move 2 birds there, and add a corridor between the islands.
materials: 8 coins or paper squares with a dot on one side
a steel plate and a tumbler
paper and a pencil for the results
general: Spend the whole budget on the plan with the most birds.
Keep everyone on one island, so the birds can find each other.
Choose the cheapest plan, so there is money left for guards.
creative: Put the birds on two islands, so one disaster cannot reach everyone.
Add a corridor, so a lost group can be replaced by the other.
Spend less on the island and more on a second place.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own plan of 6 points or less, such as 4 coins on each of two joined islands. Test it 5 times. Does it beat Plans B and D?

setup.art: Two small islands drawn on paper, joined by a thin strip, with two coins on each island and a notepad with a plan written on it.
setup.caption: 1. Plan D: two islands, two coins on each, joined by a corridor.

setup.art: A child tipping coins onto a steel plate and writing the number of heads in a table, with the island drawing beside the plate.
setup.caption: 2. Toss for each island and count the heads.

setup.art: A table of five runs for each plan, with the runs that died out circled in red.
setup.caption: 3. Circle the runs that died out and compare the plans.

flow.do: 1. Read the four plans and their costs. 2. Plan A is the Coin Years Test with 4 coins and room for 4. 3. Plan B starts with 8 coins and room for 8. 4. Plan C starts with 2 coins on each of two islands, with room for 4 on each. 5. Plan D is the same as Plan C, and a corridor refills an empty island.
flow.say: The last four birds of a species live on one island. You have 6 points to spend. Here are the four plans.
flow.kid: Read the four plans. A costs 0. B costs 6. C costs 3. D costs 5. Which will you choose?
flow.parent: The rule is the same as in the Coin Years Test. Toss the coins for each island. Each heads is 2 young. The number of coins for the next generation is twice the heads, and never more than the room. A plan ends when no birds are left on any island.
flow.context: This is the first step of Keep the Last Four Alive. Here you read the four plans and their costs.

flow.do: 1. Ask which plan will keep the birds alive the most often, and why. 2. Write down the guess and the reason. 3. Tell your child that you will test Plan B and Plan D, because you already know what Plan A does.
flow.say: Which plan do you think will keep the birds alive the most often? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which plan will keep the birds alive most often? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Plan B, because 8 birds are more than 4. (A fair guess. The test will show.)
Plan D, because the two islands protect each other.

flow.context: This step of Keep the Last Four Alive is for guessing. You guess which plan will work best, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Test Plan B 5 times. 2. Start with 8 coins. Toss them and count the heads. Double the number, and never write more than 8. 3. Toss again with that many coins. 4. Stop after 10 generations, or when the number reaches 0. 5. Write whether each run died out.
flow.say: Plan B has 8 birds on an island with room for 8. Toss the coins, double the heads, and go on for 10 generations. Do it 5 times.
flow.kid: Start with 8 coins. Toss. Double the heads. Never write more than 8. Go on for 10 generations. Do 5 runs.
flow.parent: Plan B died out in about 4 runs in 10 on a computer. In 5 runs, expect 1 to 3 to die out.
flow.context: This step of Keep the Last Four Alive tests Plan B. You run 8 birds on a bigger island, 5 times, for up to 10 generations.

flow.do: 1. Test Plan D 5 times. 2. Start with 2 coins on island A and 2 coins on island B. 3. Toss each island and count the heads. Double each number, and never write more than 4 on an island. 4. If one island has 0 and the other has 2 or more, put 2 coins on the empty island. They are birds who walked across the corridor. 5. Stop after 10 generations, or when both islands are at 0. 6. Write whether each run died out.
flow.say: Plan D has two islands with 2 birds each, and a corridor. Toss for each island. If one island is empty and the other has 2 or more, 2 birds walk across.
flow.kid: Start with 2 coins on each island. Toss each island. Double the heads. If one island is empty, 2 coins walk across.
flow.parent: Plan D died out in about 3 runs in 10 on a computer, so expect 1 or 2 to die out in 5 runs. Five runs are few, and luck can reverse the order of Plans B and D. That is worth saying aloud.
flow.context: This step of Keep the Last Four Alive tests Plan D. You run two small islands joined by a corridor, 5 times.

flow.do: 1. Count how many runs of Plan B and of Plan D died out. 2. Remember how many runs of the group of 4 died out in the Coin Years Test, which was Plan A. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 4. Ask what you would need to be sure which plan is better.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Count the runs that died out for B and for D. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Plan D cost less than Plan B. Why can it be the better plan?
good: Two islands joined by a corridor cannot be ended by one bad year in one place.
A lost group is replaced from the other island.

ask.q: Five runs of each plan are few. What would you do to be surer?
good: Do many more runs of each plan.
Combine the results of everyone in the family.

check.q: Why can two small islands with a corridor lose the birds less often than one bigger island?
options: One island can be refilled from the other
Small islands have more food
A corridor makes birds breed faster
check.why: If one island loses all its birds, the other can send 2 across. The birds are lost only if both islands are empty at once. Choosing the second answer forgets that the islands had the same rule as every other plan.

flow.context: This is the last step of Keep the Last Four Alive. You compare how often the birds died out under each plan and say why.

items.p: What does 'endemic' mean?
opts: Found naturally in only one place in the world
items.why: An endemic species lives naturally in only one place, such as one island, one lake or one range of hills. She can still be common in that place.

items.p: True or false: an endemic species is always weak.
items.why: False. A species with a small range can be well fitted to her place and live there for a very long time. The danger is that one fire, disease or dam can reach all of her at once.

items.p: All the places where a species lives are her ____.
items.why: The house crow's range covers most of India. The Narcondam hornbill's range is one small island.

items.p: Sort these species by the size of their range.
items.why: House crows, peafowl and rock pigeons live across much of India. The hornbill, the sangai deer and the lion-tailed macaque each live in only one region.

items.p: Match each species to the only place where she lives.
items.why: These four places are an island, a lake, a range of hills and one forest. A strong answer says that each one is cut off from other places like it.
pairs: one island in the Andaman Sea
in and around the Gir forest

items.p: A forest with 10 species is cut to half its size. How many species are likely to stay?
items.why: Common species live in every part of a forest, so the half that stays still holds most of them. The first to go are the rare species with a few members. Choosing exactly 5 would only be right if every species lived in just one part of the forest, and that is not so.

items.p: Which species are lost first when a forest shrinks: common or rare? Use the Shrinking Forest Test.
items.a: The rare ones are lost first. The kinds with only 1 or 2 pieces were often missing from the half that was kept. The kinds with many pieces were on every part of the sheet, so some were always left.
items.why: A strong answer uses the result: the kinds with few pieces went missing first. It says why, which is that a species with few members lives in few spots, so one cut can take all of her.

items.p: Draw a rough map of India. Mark and label the Western Ghats, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Manipur and Gir.
items.a: A rough outline of India with a strip down the west coast labelled Western Ghats, islands to the southeast labelled Andaman and Nicobar, the northeast corner labelled Manipur and the western bulge labelled Gir.
items.why: A strong map puts the Western Ghats along the west coast, the islands out in the sea to the southeast, and Gir in Gujarat. It shows that these places are far apart.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: Three of these live in only one small region. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: The hornbill, the sangai deer and the macaque each live in one region only. The house crow lives across much of South Asia.

items.p: True or false: a biodiversity hotspot is a region with many endemic plants that has already lost most of its natural plants.
items.why: True. A hotspot has at least 1,500 plant species found nowhere else, and the region has lost at least 70 out of every 100 parts of its natural plant cover. Both parts of the meaning matter.

items.p: Put the steps of the Red List in order, from least to most at risk.
items.why: The steps climb from a species who is doing well to one who is close to extinction. Extinct comes after the last step.

items.p: A species is ____ when her last member has died.
items.why: Extinction cannot be undone. A species who is gone from one country but alive elsewhere is called locally extinct.

items.p: Money for conservation is limited. Two scientists disagree about where to spend it first.

views.who: A scientist who counts endemic species
views.says: Spend it in hotspots first. A small area there holds many species who live nowhere else.

views.who: A scientist who studies grasslands and deserts
views.says: Places with fewer species still hold species found nowhere else. If we leave them out, we lose them for ever.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with? Give a reason from this lesson. Then say one thing the other scientist has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one side and uses a fact, such as 'hotspots hold more than half the world's plant species on a tiny share of the land'. It also gives the other side its due, for example that grassland species are unique and have fewer defenders.
items.why: Both views are real. Hotspots give the most species for each rupee, and other places hold species who are found nowhere else. Neither answer is wrong.

items.p: Why do islands and mountain tops hold many endemic species?
opts: Their beings are cut off from others of their kind
They have more food than other places
They are always protected by law
items.why: A group cut off for a very long time changes in its own way and can become a new species. Birds on a far island cannot easily fly back and mix with the others.

items.p: A house crow and a Narcondam hornbill each lose half of their forest. Who is in more danger, and why?
items.a: The hornbill is in more danger. All hornbills of her species live on one island, so half the forest may be half of her whole home. The crow lives in many places, so crows elsewhere are not touched.
items.why: A strong answer says that the hornbill has nowhere else to live, and that one island is one place for a storm or a disease to reach.

items.p: Which is the biggest cause of species loss today?
items.why: Scientists record the threats to each species on the Red List. Loss of habitat to farms, logging and building is listed for more species than any other threat.

items.p: Both groups had the same rule. Why did the group of 4 die out more often than the group of 16?
items.a: With only a few coins, all of them can land tails together, and then no young are raised. Sixteen coins almost never all land tails. So a small group can end by chance alone.
items.why: A strong answer says that the rule and the average were the same. Only the number of coins was different, and a small number can fall to zero by a run of bad luck.

items.p: True or false: a species can become extinct even when nobody hunts her and her habitat is safe.
items.why: True. A small group can die out by chance, for example after a few years with few young, or one disease that reaches every member.

items.p: Four coins all land tails about 1 time in ____.
items.why: Each coin lands tails half the time. 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 is 16, so all four land tails about 1 time in 16.

items.p: Sort these cases by their cause.
items.why: Each case matches one of the five main causes of species loss. A mine and a road both cut up a habitat. Catching too many fish, or killing too many tigers, is taking too many. Rats carried on a ship are a brought-in species. A medicine that poisons vultures is a kind of pollution. Warm seas that bleach corals are a changing climate.
items: A road cuts a forest in two

items.p: Two species have 150 adults each. One lives in one forest. The other lives in ten. Which is in more danger?
opts: The one in a single forest
items.why: One fire, disease or dam in a single forest can reach every member. In ten far-apart forests, some will probably be spared. Choosing 'both the same' counts only the number of adults.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
items.why: These words are needed to talk about species in danger. A strong answer can give an Indian example for each.
pairs: gone from one region but alive elsewhere
at high risk of becoming extinct
a strip of habitat joining two protected areas
land or water kept safe by law

items.p: Label what each part of the Coin Years Test stands for: a coin, heads, tails and the number 4 or 16.
a: 4 or 16: the room for adults in the place
items.why: A model is useful only when each part stands for something real. A strong answer can also name one thing the coins leave out, such as disease or a change in food.
items.art: Four blank label lines beside a coin, a pair of heads and tails faces, and a card showing 4 and 16.

items.p: Cheetahs were brought from Africa to India in 2022. Two scientists disagree about this.

views.who: A scientist who supports the project
views.says: Cheetahs once lived on India's grasslands, and people caused their extinction. Bringing them back may also win protection for grasslands.

views.who: A scientist who doubts the project
views.says: These cheetahs come from Africa. The space may be too small, and the money could save species who are still here.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with? What would you want to know before deciding? Then say one thing the other scientist has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and names something unknown, such as whether the cheetahs can live and breed in the space they have. It admits that the other side raises real points.
items.why: This is a live argument among scientists, so there is no single correct answer. A strong answer uses reasons, and says what is still unknown.

items.p: Why can a small patch of forest lose species even when nobody cuts or hunts inside it?
opts: Hot, dry wind from the open land reaches in
Rain falls less on small patches
items.why: The edge of a forest is hotter, drier and windier than the middle. In a small patch, most of the forest is edge. Species who need damp shade can no longer live there.

items.p: Put these in order, from the first event to the last.
a: A forest is cut into small patches
Each patch holds only a few animals
A disease reaches the few in one patch
items.why: Cutting makes patches. Small patches hold small groups. A small group can be ended by one bad event. When the last member dies, the species is gone from that patch.
items: A forest is cut into small patches
A disease reaches the few in one patch
Each patch holds only a few animals

items.p: Explain in three sentences why scientists want a rare species to live in more than one place.
items.a: If a species lives in only one place, one fire, disease or flood can reach all of her. In two or more places, some are likely to be spared. A group that is lost in one place can also be replaced from another.
items.why: A strong answer says that one event can reach one place, and it says that a second place is a spare. It can use the Coin Years Test, where two islands with a corridor lost the birds less often.

items.p: India counted 1,411 tigers in 2006 and 3,682 in 2022. About how many times as many is that?
items.why: Divide 3,682 by 1,411. That is a little more than 2.6, so the number rose by about 2.6 times in 16 years. Protection can work.

items.p: Three of these help a species in danger. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Joining two forests with a corridor
Counting the animals every few years
items.why: Cutting a forest into small pieces makes more edge and smaller groups, and that is a cause of species loss. The other three protect species.

items.p: True or false: a species who is extinct in one country is extinct everywhere.
items.why: False. A species who is gone from one country but alive elsewhere is locally extinct. Cheetahs became extinct in India in 1952, and they still live in Africa and Iran.

items.p: About half the species are lost when 90 in every 100 parts of a habitat go. Why are so many left?
items.a: Common species live in many parts of the habitat, so the 10 parts that are left still hold some of them. Only the rare species with few members and a small range are likely to lose every part where they lived.
items.why: A strong answer says that species are spread unevenly. The first to go are the ones with a small range. It can use the Shrinking Forest Test, where the sixteenth of the sheet still had about 3 of the 10 kinds.

items.p: A forest is made a protected area, and a village already lives inside it. Three people disagree about what should happen.

views.says: Tigers and deer need land with no cattle, no roads and no villages. Where villages moved out of some reserves, wild animals increased.

views.who: A herder who lives in the forest
views.says: My family has lived here for generations, and we guard this forest. Moving us out is unfair, and no one will watch the forest.
The law protects wildlife, and a 2006 law gives forest peoples the right to stay. I must look for a plan that respects both.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say what you still want to find out before deciding.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view or a middle path, and gives evidence, such as the Bishnoi or the Maldhari who live beside wild animals, or the reserves where animals increased after villages moved. It names something unknown, such as how many animals each choice would keep.
items.why: Scientists and communities still argue about this, so the key is to give a reason and to say what is unknown.

items.p: Which of these is protected by ordinary village people, not by a national park?
opts: A sacred grove kept by a village
items.why: Many sacred groves, such as the kavu of Kerala, have been kept by villages for hundreds of years. National parks and reserves are made and run by the state.

items.p: True or false: one large protected area always keeps more species than several small ones.
items.why: False. This is debated. A large area has less edge and holds bigger groups. Several areas in different places can be safer from one fire or one disease. Many scientists prefer large areas joined by corridors.

items.p: A strip of habitat that joins two protected areas is called a ____.
items.why: Animals can walk along a corridor from one area to the other. A group lost in one area can then be replaced from the other.

items.p: A forest patch is 1 kilometre wide. Another is 4 kilometres wide. Which keeps more damp middle for its size?
items.why: If the dry edge reaches 100 metres in, about 64 in every 100 parts of the small patch stay damp, and about 90 in every 100 parts of the large patch do. A bigger patch has more middle for its edge.

items.p: The whole slice dried only at the rim. The 16 squares dried through. What does this say about forests cut by roads?
items.a: A small piece is all edge, like the small squares of bread. The air reaches every part, so there is no damp middle left. A forest cut into small pieces can dry and heat up right through, and species who need shade are lost.
items.why: A strong answer uses the result: the small squares had no soft middle. It says that cutting makes new edges, so there is less deep forest.

items.p: Label the three parts of this tiger reserve map: the dark centre, the ring around it, and the thin strip leading away.
a: Dark centre: the core, where nobody lives
Ring around it: the buffer, where people and wildlife share the land
Thin strip: a corridor to another forest
items.why: A reserve is planned in zones. The core is kept for wildlife, the buffer lets nearby people use the land with care, and a corridor joins the reserve to another forest.
items.art: A map of a tiger reserve with a dark green centre, a light green ring and a thin green strip leading to a second forest, with three blank label lines.

items.p: Match each problem to a way of helping.
items.why: Each help answers its problem. A strong answer can say why a second group in another place protects against a single disaster.
pairs: A forest is cut into pieces
All members live in one place
a second group in another place
Nobody knows how many are left

items.p: About 1 million species are at risk, but only 2 million have names. Why can nobody say exactly how many are lost?
items.why: Nobody can count the extinction of a species who has never been named. The figure of 1 million is an estimate built from the groups that have been studied.

items.p: Put the steps of saving a species in order.
a: Scientists count her and find the number falling
The Red List places her on a step
The Red List moves her to a safer step
items.why: A species is first counted, so people know she is in trouble. Protection comes next. When the numbers grow, she can move to a safer step. This happened to the Indian rhinoceros.
items: The Red List moves her to a safer step
Scientists count her and find the number falling
The Red List places her on a step

items.p: Is a species still alive if the last members live only in a zoo? Give your view and two reasons.
items.a: It depends on what we mean. The animals are alive, but the species no longer hunts, migrates or teaches her young in the wild, so a part of her way of living is gone. A zoo group can still be a second home, and some species have been returned to the wild.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer says what a species does in the wild, such as finding food and teaching the young, and admits that a zoo group may still keep the species alive.

items.p: True or false: extinction is natural, so there is no need to try to stop it.
items.why: False, though part of it is true. Extinction has always happened, and most species who ever lived are gone. But species are now dying out far faster than new ones form, and people cause most of the loss.

items.p: Three of these are risks for a small group. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: One disease can reach every member
A few bad years can leave too few young
Close relatives must mate with each other
There is more food for each member
items.why: More food for each member helps a small group. The other three are real risks for small groups.

items.p: Draw two forests, a road and a river between them. Show where an underpass or a bridge lets animals cross.
items.a: A drawing with two forests joined by a strip of trees. Where the strip meets the road, there is a tunnel or a bridge for animals, and the same where it meets the river.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the crossing exactly where the strip of trees meets the road or the river, and shows trees on both sides so that animals can find it.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

quiz.p: Which species is found naturally only on one small island in the Andaman Sea?
quiz.why: The Narcondam hornbill lives only on Narcondam, an island of about 7 square kilometres. The other three live across much of India.

quiz.p: A species lives in only one valley. What is her biggest danger?
opts: One fire or disease can reach all of her
quiz.why: A small range means that one event can reach every member. This is why endemic species need protection and a second home.

quiz.p: A forest loses half of its area. Which species are most likely to be lost first?
opts: Those with few members in a few places
quiz.why: Species with few members live in few spots, so one cut can take all of them. Common species live all over, so some are always left.

quiz.p: Which part of a forest patch is hotter, drier and windier?
quiz.why: Dry wind and sun reach in from the open land. This is called the edge effect, and a small patch is mostly edge.

quiz.p: True or false: a group of 4 animals and a group of 16 are equally likely to die out by chance.
quiz.why: False. All 4 coins land tails about 1 time in 16, but all 16 land tails about 1 time in 65,000. A small group can end by chance much more easily.

quiz.p: Two islands are joined by a corridor. Why do they lose all their animals less often than two islands with none?
opts: A lost group can be replaced from the other island
quiz.why: If one island is emptied, animals can walk across from the other. Both islands must be empty at once for the species to be lost.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT one of the five main causes of extinction today?
quiz.why: The five causes are habitat loss, taking too many, brought-in species, pollution and a changing climate. Protected areas help species.

quiz.p: What does 'Critically Endangered' mean on the Red List?
opts: Extremely high risk of becoming extinct
quiz.why: It is the highest step of risk before Extinct. The great Indian bustard and the gharial are on it.

opts: It joins two protected areas so animals can walk between them
It keeps all people out of a forest
It counts the animals in a forest
It stops the rain from falling
quiz.why: A corridor is a strip of habitat. A group lost in one area can be replaced from the other, and animals can find food and mates.

quiz.p: Which kind of protected area in India is the strictest, with no farming or grazing inside?
quiz.why: National parks are the most strictly protected. In a sanctuary, some uses by local people, such as grazing, may be allowed.

quiz.p: Which of these shows ordinary people protecting nature in India?
opts: Women of Assam guarding nests of hargila storks
A ship bringing rats to an island
A road cutting a forest in two
quiz.why: The Hargila Army, a group of women led by the biologist Purnima Devi Barman, protects nesting storks. Many forests are alive today because ordinary people protected them.

quiz.p: True or false: scientists know exactly how many species have died out in the last 50 years.
quiz.why: False. Most species have never been named or counted, so nobody can count exactly. Scientists build estimates from the groups they have studied.

The Red List helps governments and scientists decide which species need help first.

open_questions.q: How many species live on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: About 2 million have names. Estimates of the real number go from about 9 million to much higher, because most insects, fungi and deep-sea animals are unknown.

open_questions.q: How fast are species going extinct right now?
open_questions.why_open: Most species have never been counted, so nobody can say exactly how many are lost. Careful estimates all find a rate much higher than before people spread over the Earth.

open_questions.q: Is one large protected area better than several small ones?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have argued about this since 1975. The answer seems to depend on the species, the place, and the risk of one disaster.

open_questions.q: Should a species lost from one country be brought back from another country?
open_questions.why_open: The cheetah project in India is still young. Scientists do not agree on whether African cheetahs can fill the place of the lost Indian cheetahs.

open_questions.q: How should people choose which species to save first?
open_questions.why_open: Some say save the most species for each rupee. Others say save the species nobody else can save. Each choice leaves some species out.

open_questions.q: How long can a very small group live on, and can they ever recover?
open_questions.why_open: Some species have grown back from fewer than 200 animals, but others have not. Scientists are still working out how many are enough.

maths.problem: One coin lands tails half the time. Four coins all land tails about 1 time in 16. How many times in 65,536 would all 16 coins land tails?
maths.explain: Each extra coin halves the chance. Four coins give 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16. Sixteen coins give 2 multiplied by itself 16 times, which is 65,536. So all 16 land tails about 1 time in 65,536, far more rarely than 1 in 16.
maths.context: This is about the Coin Years Test. A group of 4 died out in most runs, and a group of 16 seldom did.
maths.why_maths: The numbers show why a group of 4 is risky and a group of 16 is safe: chance shrinks fast as the group grows.

maths.problem: In a made-up test, the part of the forest kept was 16 times smaller than the whole. The kinds fell from 10 to 3.3. How many times fewer kinds were there?
maths.explain: Divide 10 by 3.3. That is about 3. The area fell 16 times, but the kinds fell only about 3 times. So a much smaller forest still holds a fair share of the kinds.
maths.context: This is about the Shrinking Forest Test. The numbers are made up to match what the test usually gives.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two ratios shows that species fall more slowly than area, which is why the first cut looks harmless.

maths.problem: A hill is a triangle 20 centimetres wide and 10 centimetres high. A cold-loving frog lives in the top 4 centimetres, which is a triangle 8 centimetres wide. What share of the hill is that?
maths.explain: The area of a triangle is width x height ÷ 2. The whole hill is 20 x 10 ÷ 2 = 100 square centimetres. The top is 8 x 4 ÷ 2 = 16 square centimetres. So the top is 16 in every 100 parts of the hill.
maths.context: This is about the Cold Hilltop. There you draw a hill and find the area of the cool zone.
maths.why_maths: The area shows how much land a mountain species has, and how little is left when the cool zone moves up.

maths.problem: The forest owlet was not recorded after 1884. In 1997 she was found alive again in Maharashtra. For how many years was she missing?
maths.explain: Subtract the years: 1997 - 1884 = 113. So the forest owlet was missing for 113 years.
maths.context: This is about species who were thought to be extinct. The card on extinction tells how the forest owlet was found again.
maths.why_maths: A long gap shows why it is hard to be sure a species is gone.

maths.problem: India counted 1,411 tigers in 2006 and 3,682 in 2022. On average, how many more tigers were counted each year? Round to the nearest whole number.
maths.explain: The rise is 3,682 - 1,411 = 2,271. The time is 2022 - 2006 = 16 years. 2,271 ÷ 16 is about 142. So the count rose by about 142 tigers each year.
maths.context: This is about protection working. The card on what most scientists agree on gives these two counts.
maths.why_maths: An average rate lets you compare how fast a number grows over many years.

maths.problem: All 4 coins landing tails is 1 in 16. All 5 is 1 in 32. All 6 is 1 in 64. How many coins make all tails rarer than 1 in 1,000?
maths.explain: Each extra coin doubles the number. 64, 128, 256, 512, 1,024. That is 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 coins. With 10 coins, all tails is 1 in 1,024, which is rarer than 1 in 1,000. With 9 coins it is 1 in 512.
maths.context: This is about the Coin Years Test, where a group of coins can all land tails together.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the doubling pattern tells you how many members a group needs before chance alone is unlikely to end it.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that a patch of forest loses species even when nobody cuts or hunts inside it? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1970s, many people thought that a patch of forest would keep its animals as long as nobody cut the trees or hunted inside. Scientists argued about whether one large reserve or several small ones would be better, but nobody had tested it. In 1979 an American biologist, Thomas Lovejoy, began a test in the Amazon rainforest near Manaus in Brazil. Cattle farmers there were clearing forest, and the law made them leave some standing. Lovejoy asked them to leave square patches of 1, 10 and 100 hectares. His team counted the birds, trees and insects in each patch before the forest around it was cut. Then they kept counting, year after year. The patches lost species, though nobody touched them. Hot, dry wind blew in from the open land. Trees near the edge died for 100 metres or more into the forest. The smallest patches lost many of their forest birds within about 15 years. The test is still running. It showed that a protected area must be large, or joined to others.
how_we_found_out.who: Thomas Lovejoy, an American biologist, with Brazilian and other scientists of the forest fragments project near Manaus
how_we_found_out.when: The test began in 1979 and is still running. The result on forest birds was published in 2003.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a patch of forest keeps all its species as long as nobody cuts or hunts inside. The Amazon patches lost species because they were small and had dry, windy edges.
how_we_found_out.art: A square patch of tall rainforest standing alone in a cleared cattle field, with a few scientists carrying notebooks walking towards it.

roots.context: We have learned why rare species need protected places, and how a small group can be lost by chance. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Coin Years Test, 4 coins all landed tails far more often than 16 coins did. Nobody hunted either group, and the rule was the same. A species lasts only while enough of her members live in enough places. So a species survives because many members live together in many places. One member alone cannot keep the species going.
deep_truth.habit: We speak of 'the tiger' or 'the hornbill' as if she were one animal who is safe or in danger. A species is a whole group spread over places, and the risk belongs to the group. One strong animal does not make a species safe.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Coin Years Test, groups of 4 and 16 followed the same rule, but the group of 4 died out far more often. On a computer, about 3 out of every 4 groups of 4 animals died out within 10 generations. Only about 1 out of every 8 groups of 16 animals did. In 2018, 23 lions died in a few weeks in the Gir forest, where all the wild lions of Asia live.

three.who_am_i: You belong to a species of about 8 billion members, living on every continent. No single flood or fire can reach all of us. A species of 600 lions in one forest has no such safety.
three.what_is_life: Life goes on because parents have young, and the young grow up and have young of their own. A species is a long line of such families that may have run for thousands or millions of years. It ends when the last member dies without leaving young.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is made of many places, and each place holds beings found nowhere else. When a place is lost, what lived only there is lost with it.

roots.thread: All living beings share one ancestor, so every species is a branch of one tree of life. When a group is cut off on an island or a hilltop for a very long time, a new branch can form, and the new species lives nowhere else. That is how one life became many kinds. A branch can also be lost, and when the last member dies, that kind is gone for ever. The rest of the tree goes on with fewer branches.

practice.say: Sit still and find one living being near you, such as a crow, a potted plant or an ant. Look at her for three slow breaths. playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through but not tried at home. I checked the numbers by computer. For the Coin Years Test, I ran the rule 200,000 times: a group of 4 died out within 10 generations in about 3 runs in 4, and a group of 16 in about 1 run in 8. With two islands of 4, both were empty in about 11 runs in 20 with no corridor and about 4 in 20 with a corridor. In Keep the Last Four Alive, Plan A died out in about 3 runs in 4, Plan B in about 4 in 10 and Plan D in about 3 in 10, so five runs of each plan can reverse the order and the step says so. The Shrinking Forest Test gives about 8, 6, 5 and 3 kinds out of 10 on the half, quarter, eighth and sixteenth of the sheet, which I worked out from the chance that a kind of that size lies on that part. In Same Count, Different Forest, a sample of 8 pieces shows about 6 kinds from the even bowl and about 3 from the uneven bowl. The Bread Forest needs fresh bread and a fan, and it is slower in the monsoon, so the step says to leave it longer then. The Cold Hilltop is a paper triangle, and a real hill is not one, which the step says. In Two Safe Squares, I checked every pair of squares by computer: D and F save 10 of the 12 species, and the two richest squares save 8. A Way Through has a cheapest cost of 7 on the map given, with two routes of that cost, and two squares that would raise the cost to 9. The species, forest and map in the games are made up. Real-world facts checked on 17 Nov 2026: Gir lions (674 in 2020), tiger counts, hotspot numbers, Chipko at Reni, Silent Valley dates, Guru Jambheshwar and the Corbett and cheetah dates held up. Softened: the Khejarli toll is now 'about 363 are said to have died', the bustard count is now about 130 and the Narcondam hornbill about a thousand, the hargila nests are now about 28 to about 200, and India's share of species is 7 or 8 in 100.
